speechtext:
I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Galliher :
That that portion of the 16th report of the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines reporting the preamble of the Bill (Nio. 157) to incorporate the Brandon, Saskatchewan and Hudson Bay Railway Company, not proven ; be referred back to the said committee for further consideration.
This Bill came up at the end of the meeting of the Railway Committee to-day and when the motion on the preamble was put by the Chairman I demanded that the yeas and nays be taken. The requisite number of members stood up, but the Chairman did not take the yeas and nays and declared the preamble lost. I consider that the Bill should go back for further consideration.

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I might explain, that in the absence of the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) I acted as Chairman of the Railway Committee this morning. The question was put to the committee whether the preamble should be adopted or not on three different occasions

and each time the committee answered almost unanimously against the preamble. At the request of my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) I asked the gentlemen who were in the committee to rise for and against the preamble. Five members were in favour of the preamble and fifteen against. Then the hon. gentleman asked that the yeas and nays be taken. One o'clock sounded and I declared the preamble lost. I suggested to the hon. gentleman that the yeas and nays be taken as the members would rise from their seats, because I would have to call the whole list otherwise, which I thought was not necessary. The sentiment of the committee was taken and it was nearly unanimously against the preamble.

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I may say that I was one of the live who stood up in favour of the preamble. The facts are as stated by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) who was Chairman of the committee, but in seconding the motion I may say that if my hon. friend (Mr. Davis) thinks that some-I would hardly call it injustice has been done him-if he thinks it would be fairer to him to take the yeas and nays in the usual way I do not see any objection to that being done. I am bound to say that the feeling of the committee seemed to be against the Bill at the time, but nevertheless I think that the Bill should be referred back in order that it may receive the usual treatment.

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
From the moment this Bill was introduced in the committee the sentiment of the members was clearly against it. No attempt was made by the promoter of the Bill to show that there was any probability of the road being constructed. The clause describing the route was so badly worded that it was impossible for the members of the committee to determine where at least one branch of the road was intended to be run. The Chairman of the committee has stated the case very fairly. There was a clear response from the committee in the ordinary way signifying nay to the preamble. As the Chairman of the committee has stated only five members rose in favour of it and fifteen in opposition. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) no doubt did ask for the yeas and nays, and the Chairman of the committee fairly offered to have the yeas and nays taken in the way he has described-not in the usual way, by calling the roll, and each man responding for himself, but by asking those who were in favour of the preamble to stand up, and the clerk would record their names, intending then to ask those who were opposed to the preamble to rise in order that their names might be recorded by the clerk, just as a vote in this chamber is recorded by the clerk of the House. This would have saved considerable time, as it could have been Mr. LEMIEUX (Gaspe).
done much more quickly-the hour of one o'clock having nearly arrived-than calling a roll of 150 or 160 names, the greater majority of whom were absent. To my mind the committee expressed its opinion, and expressed it very decidedly as being opposed to the granting of this charter, and I see no reason for asking that the Bill be referred back any more than any other Bill which had not received the approval of the Railway Committee. I consider that the Chairman of the committee acted with all fairness to the promoter of the Bill, and the yeas and nays would have been recorded in the manner I have indicated had not the hon. member for Saskatchewan himself decidedly objected.

maintopic: BRANDON, SASKATCHEWAN AND HUDSON BAY RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I suppose I may have a word in closing this discussion. As to the merits of the Bill, I do not think they are before us at the present time, although the hon. gentleman has seen fit to go into them. The case is this. The chairman of the committee seems to have got it into his head that it is a standing rule that the committee should adjourn at one o'clock. So far as I know, there is no such rule at all, and when I asked for the yeas and nays I think I had a right to do so ; and I now ask that the Bill be sent back, because of its not having been fairly treated in that respect.
Motion agreed to.

On section 184,

This section stood over. I propose to change the section, acting upon the suggestion of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). I will read the clause as it will stand, if amended as I propose :
The railway may be carried upon, along or across any existing highway upon leave therefor having been first obtained from the board as hereinafter provided. But the board shall not grant leave to any company to carry any street railway or tramway or any railway operated or to be operated as a street railway or Mr. BELL.
tramway, along any highway which is within the limits of any city or incorporated town until the company shall have first obtained the_ consent therefor by a by-law of the municipal authority of such city or incorporated town.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
I am not opposing that amendment so far as it goes ; but it only goes half way, in my opinion. That emphasizes the fact, if any emphasis were required-and I do not think it was necessary-that, so far as this Act is concerned a steam railway could be operated along any highway without the consent of the municipality. I greet with appreciation the amendment suggested by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) and I congratulate the minister upon accepting it. But while I entirely agree with it, I am even more opposed to steam railways running upon highways of municipalities than I am to electric tramway's. This section provides that a railway may be carried upon, along, or across any existing highway. This section was changed from its original form. The hon. minister said it was only the difference between tweedledum and tweedle-dee, but I am confident that I am right in saying that as the clause originally stood, the onus was more in favour of the railway company exercising this right-this pretended right-than it was under the old Act. I desire to amend this section by striking out the words ' upon, along or ' in the first subsection as amended by the minister. Under my amendment a railway could not be carried upon or along the highway, but could only cross it. Without detaining the committee at length with my reasons, I may say that the principle I advocate is the same as" that favoured by the hon. member for West Toronto and the gentleman with whom he has been advising in getting the minister to accept the amendment providing that tramways or electric roads should not be allowed to operate in municipalities without the consent of the municipal authorities. But, with all due deference, I would suggest that if the committee were to accept my amendment, there would be no need for the amendment of the hon. member for West Toronto, for it would prevent the operation of any railway upon a highway in any municipality not only cities and towns without the consent of those who own the highway. Now, I am bound to emphasize to-day the point I made when this matter was under discussion before, because, the more I think of it the more sure I am that I am right. My contention is that this parliament has no right to empower anvbody to interfere with the highways, except so far as it may be necessary for carrying on a work which this parliament has the power to authorize. The highways are vested in the provincial authorities and are delegated by them to the municipal authorities. This parliament is ultra vires if it attempts, without the consent of the provincial and municipal authorities, to interfere with these highways, unless for the

necessary work of carrying out an undertaking which this parliament has the power to authorize. I wish to put myself clear with the committee, 1 state plainly that this parliament can authorize a railway to he built and can authorize the use of the highway necessary for the construction of that railway ; but, any use of the highway that is not necessary for the construction of the railway cannot be authorized by this parliament. If it is not necessary for the railway to cross a highway, this parliament has no power to say upon what terms the municipal authorities shall allow the use of the highway. If further argument were necessary, I might point out to the House what the Ontario Railway Law is. That Act is passed by the provincial legislature which controls the highway. It provides that no railway shall be carried along existing highways and shall only cross a highway without the consent of the proper municipal authorities. When we consider how the provincial authorities here guard the rights of the people on the highways, may we not ask ourselves if we are not doing an almost outrageous thing in undertaking to authorize the Railway Committee, which is the creature of this parliament, to allow railways to pass upon or along highways without the consent of the municipal authorities ? This provincial law that I have quoted is the enactment of that authority which, under the British North America Act, owns and controls the highway. That authority has seen fit to enact that no railway shall go along or upon the highway, but may merely cross the same without the consent of the municipal authorities. And we are asked to enact here, as if we knew what we were doing, that a railway may not only cross, but may run upon and along a highway if the commissioners, who derive their authority only from this parliament, choose to say so. As I said the other day, there is no doubt in my mind that we are passing legislation that we have no power to pass in attempting to interfere with the highway without the consent of the municipal authorities or the provincial authorities from which the municipalities get their power. We have the right to control so far as it is necessary for the carrying out of any work that we have the power to authorize!" It is necessary for any railway almost to cross highways. But our legislation is ultra vires if it goes further. The House may be willing and the minister may be willing to pass such legislation ; but though I cannot stop them, I am bound to put myself upon record as clearly as I can, giving my reasons, in protest against such legislation, first upon the ground that it is ultra vires of this parliament. Besides the question of whether it is intra vires or ultra vires, I want to point out that in my judgment it would be a very improvident and improper thing for this parliament to undertake to interfere with
the control of highways, because that would at once involve a contest with the provincial legislature as well as with the municipal authorities. The municipal authorities are given their power by the provincial legislature to say what shall be done with the highways and who shall control them. We all know that if a highway is out of repair the municipal authorities are responsible for the consequences, any township that is incorporated is responsible for keeping its highways in good repair, it is bound to protect travellers in passage over the highway, to keep the highways open and in proper use for the public, and it has this control by authority given it by the provincial legislature. So that outside the question of whether the provision is intra vires or ultra vires, it would be improvident for us to undertake to say, by a commission which we constitute, that any interference can be made with these highways without the consent of the municipal authorities, or of the provincial legislature which gives that power to the municipal authorities.
As I said a moment ago, a railway must sometimes cross a highway, but it need not do any more. If it is desired to use the highway for any other purpose than merely to cross it, it must be because the railway is going to try to do something that the municipality does not want it to do. If it is necessary to give a railway power to do more than cross a highway, if it is wanted to give this commission power to enable a railway to. do more than cross a highway, it must be because the railway may want to force their way along a Wigliway and do something more than merely to cross it without the consent of those who control the highway. That, I say, is something this parliament ought not to be a party to ; and in my judgment, if a case of conflict should arise and was carried to the highest court of the empire, this authority proposed to be given would be decided to be ultra vires. Therefore, I move to strike out these words ' upon, along or,' so that the railway may only cross an existing highway That is plenty of power to give these commissioners. They may have to decide under what terms the railway shall cross a highway, because that may be necessary. I want, moreover, to tell the minister that the Electric Railway Act of the province of Ontario also provides the same thing. There is a General Railway Act in the province of Ontario relating to steam railways, and as near as you can make it, their legislation is analogous to the Act now before us. That is the General Railway Act that has always been in force before we had any electric railways, and which I have quoted. There is also an Electric Railway Act which does not even allow electric railways to be used upon highways without the consent of the municipal authorities. So that if this legislation passes, undertaking in this wide

way to allow these commissioners to give power to railways to interfere with the provincial and municipal control of highways, there is going to be trouble made in this country that will take a great deal of expense and a good many years of litigation, perhaps, finally to decide ; and there is no doubt in my opinion that it will be held to be ultra vires. But, as I said, even if it is not so held, it is an improvident and wrong thing for us to interfere with the municipal control of highways.

I think I have stated more than once that I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman's views that this power is one which the parliament of Canada cannot lawfully exercise. I think the power is intra vires of the parliament of Canada, and I think this power may be more than assumed when we remember all the years that this law has been upon the statute-book.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That does not prove anything.
I say it does. It proves that no one has ever thought it worth while to raise the contention in all the controversies that have arisen, and they have been innumerable.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has that question ever arisen ?

If it has arisen, it has never been carried to any court; and if no body has raised the question in the courts that this provision is ultra vires of the parliament of Canada, I say there is almost an irresistible presumption that if any lawyer had thought that the point could be successfully raised it would have been raised long before this. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I have no hesitation at all in promoting this legislation so far as its being within the legislative competency of this parlianient is concerned. Now, I readily consented to the amendment which the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) asked me to consider, because it had reference to the question of the operation of electric tramways within cities and towns. I think there is a very good case to be made out in favour of the fullest authority being vested in the municipal corporation of the city or town to say whether, where, when and how their streets should be occupied. When an aggregation of people are crowded into a large town or city, the dangers, risks, annoyances and property losses that are often occasioned by these railways, are of such importance, and the questions raised are of such magnitude, municipally speaking, that I think it well the corporate authority of such city or town should be consulted before these works are laid down. Moreover, I do not myself sympathize very Mr. LANCASTER.
heartily with the idea of this parliament concerning itself with legislation respecting the construction and operation of tramways in cities. These are essentially local questions, and I do not think, except in the most exceptional cases, that parliament ought to give any countenance at all to the requests made to us to legislate respecting them. These are the two reasons which led me to accept the suggestion that was offered by the hon. member for Toronto.
Now, I cannot go any further. I cannot go to the extent which the hon. gentleman asks me to go, because I think it would be unwise to do so. I have had a good deal of experience as to the operation of this clause respecting highways generally throughout the country, during the years in which I have acted on the Railway Committee, and I know of no instance in which the Railway Committee was called upon to-decide these cases in which we had not before us the representatives of the city, town or other municipal corporation, and in which we did not hear their objections, if they had any, and gave them every consideration. There is no doubt at all that the commission would act exactly in the same way. They would have no interest in doing anything else than to meet the reasonable wishes and the reasonable objections which these municipal officers might make. Now when you are reasonably assured that the commission will exercise all due care, it is not well to treat this question as if they would only desire to meet the wishes of the railway company without any regard to the views of the municipal authorities. It is not well to treat the question in that way, in view of the fact that this parliament has. during its existence, thought it well that this power should reside somewhere of determining whether or not a railway should use a public highway in any given case. That power I think ought to continue to reside in some supreme authority. I think, therefore, it would be unwise for parliament to say that all the highways of the country should be excluded from use by railway corporations unless and until the municipal authorities gave permission to use them. I hope the hon. gentleman will not press his motion, because, if he does, it will be my duty to ask the committee to reject it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I know there is a good deal in what the minister has said, but I desire to say that I had considered all these things before I made this motion. I am not saying for a minute but what the Railway Committee in the past has considered" the municipality's representations, but there is a difference between the municipality being the judge of the case as distinguished from being one of the parties interested. The hon. minister's enactment would put the municipality down as one of the parties whose rights were in dispute

and who is at the mercy of the railway commission. I say that the municipality's position is beyond that. The municipality controls the highway and this parliament has no right to say that we will allow you to control the highway if you do what we tell you, and we will be the judge as to the manner in which you control it. This railway commission will look at the question as a board composed of honest men acting in the interests of the whole of Canada. It may consider that in the interests of Canada it would be necessary to force some municipality, whether city or town, or village or township, to allow a steam railway to run up its main street. The commission might say :	We know that
it makes ducks and drakes out of the town, we know it is going to ruin your principal business street, we know it is going to destroy your town, we know it is going to disarrange everything and cause the people to; pull up stakes and leave, we know that this is against the wishes of everybody in the neighbourhood, but in the interests of the railway which is going to run from the Atlantic to the Pacific, or, it may be, a shorter distance, and because it would cost them too much money to go anywhere else, you must allow them to use your main street to get through the town. Has not the municipality the right to say :	We do not
want the railway here ? You must buy your way if you are going through the town and you cannot use our main street for the purposes of the road. They have the power under the law to say that they do not want their streets used for* railway purposes. This parliament has the right to say that the municipality shall not have the right to interfere with the railway going aloug and that it must allow the l-ailway to cross the street. That commission can force a municipality to allow a railway to cross its streets and there is provision made in the Act for all the machinery necessary to carry out that authority. But, to go further and say that a municipality is wrong in not allowing its streets to be used for railway purposes and to say that this commission shall have power to say that it will override the municipality's wishes and to force the municipality to allow its streets to be used for railway purposes is placing power where it has no right to be and where this parliament cannot put it. By assuming authority we do not give ourselves that authority. The British North America Act has settled that question. By passing an Act saying that we can do this we do not make our Act any more valid or binding, even if it had been in existence for fifty years, if. we did not have the power. This question has never been decided by the highest court and I am still of the opinion that if it were decided the Act would be held to be ultra vires in so far as it forces a municipality to allow its streets to be used against its will by any authority constituted 165
by this parliament. Although the hon. minister is very willing now to allow some of the municipalities to control electric roads which are matters of local importance in his opinion does the hon. minister think that an electric road is as dangerous, as obnoxious and as damaging for a municipality to have upon its streets as a steam railway ? The municipality should, I admit, have control of electric roads and it should not be obliged to have electric roads run along its streets without its consent. The hon. minister believes that is right and says that the Bill is now to be amended in order that it shall not interfere with the municipality's control of its streets in so far as electric railways or tramways are concerned, because he thinks the municipality should have control over them. That being the case I ask this committee to say how much more ought we to say that the municipalities ought to be consulted and not the board of railway commissioners as to whether or not a steam railway shall run upon its streets or highways. With all deference to the hon. minister and because I believe X am right upon this question I cannot withdraw my amendment and I must ask the committee to pass upon it.

On section 206-appointment of inspecting engineers,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I notice that this section provides that inspecting engineers may be appointed by the minister or the board.
I think it would be better to confine that appointment to the responsible minister, as it is not, I suppose, a matter of immediate urgency at any time.

There is no doubt that it is well for the minister to have the power of ap-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
pointing an inspecting engineer with the approval of Council; but there are many duties devolving upon the board which make it important that they also should have that power. Some sudden emergency might call for the immediate appointment of an inspecting engineer, during the absence of the minister, and it would very much tie the hands of the board if they were not empowered to make such an appointment, as it is their duty to see that the provisions of the Act are carried out, and that the safety and security of the railways are looked after.

speechtext: Perhaps I do not quite apprehend the way these appointments are made. The hon. gentleman will observe that the approval of council will be necessary to the appointment by the board as well as by the minister. Of course, the minister, representing the Railway Department, would make the recommendation just as he does now. I apprehend that the hon. gentleman is right in thinking that there would have to be a small staff of permanent engineers from whom the inspecting engineers employed by the board would be taken. I think it would be well, however, that they should be persons recommended by the board.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it contemplated that the board may appoint an engineer in any certain locality to inspect any specific piece of work rather than take an engineer a long distance to do it 7

That is the intention.
On section 207, subsection 4.-inspection of railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That makes the board absolutely bound by the report of the engineer.
If the board is not satisfied with his report, they can send another engineer or two others to revise it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Even though the inspecting engineer did not report favourably, it would be better to let the board take the responsibility of deciding on the question. They might give a conditional order. They might give an order to allow the company to open for freight and not for passengers.

In actual practice it would happen more frequently that the road is open before it is quite ready than that a refusal to allow it to open is given when it is. My experience is that companies say their road is in working shape and ready to be passed, and when we send out our engineers they report, in quite a number of instances that it is not. The engineer states the reasons why he considers the road not ready ; and if his reasons are not considered sufficient, the board can send out another officer. But as a rule it will be found that the engineer's report will state the facts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I know as a fact that sometimes an engineer is sent out by the department who may not be a man of great experience. He goes 400 or 500 miles to inspect a bit of work, he is unfavourably impressed and makes an adverse report, and you give notice to the company. Surely it would be better to say that the company's engineer and the inspecting engineer should appear before the board and the board should hear both parties and take the responsibility of deciding.

This does not give the board a fair opportunity of having the question decided whether the railway is ready or not. If the clause were worded so that the inspector would make a report to the board and the board would hear both parties, that would give protection to the public and the necessary degree of protection to the company. It might happen that the engineer would be a young man, technical, very zealous, and make an adverse report, and although he may have to state the facts on which his judgment is founded, yet it should be left to the board to consider the whole matter and give its decision, I would suggest that the latter part of the clause be amended.

The section provides that the engineer shall state the grounds for his opinion and the company shall be entitled to notice thereof, and the board shall refuse such application in whole or in part, and may direct a further inspection and report.

I would be willing to strike out the word ' shall ' and insert the word ' may.'
I move that the word ' shall ' in forty-seventh line be struck out and the word ' may ' inserted in its place.

Amendment agreed to.
On section 211. Safety appliances on trains.

The opening words of this section are 'every company shall provide and cause to be used on all trains the best and most efficient obtainable apparatus, appliances and means.' I move that this be altered to read ' modern and efficient apparatus ' and so on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would not the words ' most efficient ' be better ?

Of course, the supposition is that the latest is the best. I think it will be found that when the company gets modern things they will get the best things, otherwise they would not continue to use them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It would appear to have the effect of compelling them almost to get the most modern, though they may not be the best.
I think it is paring down the old Act a little too much. The appliances may be perfectly modern and still not be safe.
They have got to be, not only modern, but efficient.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The old Act said that they must use such apparatus as would ' afford good and sufficient means.' There is a little difference between efficient and sufficient. It might be modern and efficient, yet not be as good as possible.
It would be hardly fair to compel the railway company to use the best apparatus, so long as they used one that Is efficient.

I do not think it reasonable to ask the company to be constantly changing. But I would call the minister's attention to this point, that unless he sees some good reason for changing the wording of the old Act, it is inadvisable to make an alteration. He knows perfectly well that we have had from time to time judicial decisions upon these statutes, as they have been in force for a long time ; they have received a judicial construction, and it is unsafe to make an alteration In the wording unless there is a necessity for it.

The hon. gentleman is right in his general proposition, and I have not violated the spirit of the principle, so far as I know. I think that where the words have acquired a distinct meaning and have been found to answer all purposes, it is desirable to retain them. But in the present instance I think there is a good reason for making a change in the construction of this section. The words ' good and sufficient ' are not terms that I think have been subjected to any judicial interpretation. I think they could be improved, I think the word ' efficient ' is better than ' sufficient,' it is a stronger term, and we need not hesitate to use strong terms when we are regulating the means of guarding life and property more securely. The word ' modern ' is not open to the interpretation that some gentlemen have put upon it. It does not mean that all apparatus must necessarily be of modern invention ; it only means that it must be of modern use, that it must be an up-to-date apparatus, an apparatus which is used generally on first class railways. Railways are using a good many devices that are efficient, and yet are very old ; that is, they have been invented a long time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the words * best and most efficient obtainable ' correctly express what we want to bring about.

It is hardly fair to say that every railway should be compelled to use the very best, because the best might be more than efficient ; it might be very expensive, and it would be unduly loading a railway to require the company to go to the expense of getting the very best, when an up-to-date and an efficient appliance would be all that is required, all that anybody could reasonably ask for. There are grades in value and grades in cost, and when you ask them to use the very best, you are taking an extreme ground.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I agree with the minister that it would be unfair to compel the company to be constantly changing and to adopt the latest invention, merely because it was the most modern. If they procure what is the best at the time, that ought to be in compliance with the Act. But I call the hon. minister's attention again to this matter, and I think there is more reason now than I thought of when I was speaking before for preserving the wording of the old Act. We have had a number of decisions in regard to setting fire.
There are provisions later on covering that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Are there express provisions 1
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If there are specific provisions as the hon. minister says in reference to railway engines throwing fire, I do not know that I have any objection to this particular clause.
There is a good deal in what the hon. gentleman says, where you require the best or most efficient appliances. Would not that apply in case of fire to the other ?
That comes later on. This section relates more particularly to the means of making travel secure for passengers on trains.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is very important not to use words here that would imply that the appliances must be effectual for the purpose ; otherwise, you would make the railway the guarantor of the safety of passengers. It has never been held that they must provide appliances that will effect these objects. They can only do their best to do so.

I thing the word ' efficient ' is not objected to. I have had it under discussion with railway people, both the employers and the operating staff, and they see no objection to the word ' efficient.' I beg to move that subsection (a) be amended by striking out the word ' the ' before the word ' train ' in the second line and substituting the word * any passenger.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does not the hon. minister think it would be well to leave it as it is ? Of course, the consequences of an accident to a freight train are not so dis-asti'ous as in the case of a passenger train, but still there are lives upon a freight train. The safety of a freight train requires that communication shall be easily obtainable between the conductor and the engine driver. The wreck of a freight train for want of such communication might cause a disaster to a passenger train in which many lives might be lost.
It would not be practicable to make this provision apply to freight trains. There is nothing yet devised to provide sucli communication.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is a bell-rope on most freight trains.

It is a very short freight train on which there is a bell-rope. When you come to haul fifty or sixty cars, some flat cars and some box cars, you will find it quite impossible to have a rope that can be relied upon. That is the universal judgment of railway people. I know it is the judgment of our own people. I have had occasion to have the subject considered by them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does this cover the case of a mixed train ?

Yes, any train that is taking passengers. I beg to move also :
That subsection (bj be amended by striking out. in 'line five, all the words from ' including' to the word ' possible ' in the eighth line and submitting the following : ' Including the'power, drive wheel, brake and appliances for operating the train brake system upon the locomotive and having a sufficient number of cars in every train so equipped with power or train brakes that the engineer on the locomotive drawing such train can control the speed or bring it to a stop in the quickest and best manner possible without requiring the brakesman to use the common hand-brake for that purpose.
These clauses which are being incorporated in the Bill now are clauses which are to be found in a Bill introduced during the present session which was promoted by some of the railway employees.
Subsection, as amended, agreed to.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS Aim) *CANALS. I move to strike out subsections 3 and 4 and to insert after the word ' train ' in the second line :
Couplers which couple automatically by impact and which can be uncoupled without the necessity of going in between the cars.
I move to strike out in subsections (d) and (e) lines 11 to 15 and to substitute therefor :
Provided that the company shall not be obliged to equip all trains with the power drive wheel brake or air-brakes as provided in subsection *(d) of this section, nor to equip the cars with automatic couplers as provided in subsection (c) of this section before ithe first day of January, 1906.
I may say that the association wished the limit to he 1905 and the railways wanted it 1907, and I think that perhaps we arrived at a fair date by taking 1906.

speechtext: Suppose that some improved appliances were discovered, they would still have to go on using these appliances.

Yes. This House of Commons passed a Bill once if not twice containing this power brake clause, and it seems to favour the idea that it should be used. We are therefore not making a new departure. I propose to ask the committee to insert in subsection 2 the following :
Every company shall adopt and use upon all of its rolling stock such height of draw-bars as the board may determine in accordance with any standard from time to time adopted by competent railway authorities.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What does the minister mean by a competent railway authority ? Would it be Sir William Van Horne, or Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, or Mr. Hays ?

What is called the Master Car Builders' Association regulates these things generally. It is a United States organization, and I did not like to mention the name in the Bill, but it does regulate all these questions as to what shall be the standard with regard to such appliances.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the Master Oar Builders of the United States adopted some patent, we would have to follow them, although we might have a better one of our own. Would it not be better to leave this to the commissioners than to some railway authority which nobody knows ?
The Master Car Builders are an association of very high standing. That is a general name given to a sort of final railway court of appeal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I want to call attention to a point which I mentioned the other day. It is not for the purpose of obstructing the measure, because we are all anxious to get through with it as soon as possible. I do not know how it may be with the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hng-gart) and the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), both of whom, I believe, are familiar with railway matters and railway law' ; but I may tell the hon. minister that, although I am very anxious to follow' these matters, with these amendments coming in without any previous notice, it is impossible for me to grasp their meaning so as to know whether they are such as we ought to agree to or not. I suggested the other day that if the hon. minister would furnish the hon. lender of the opposition with half a dozen ' copies of proposed amendments, where tiiey

are long, this would enable us to give him the benefit of our views, which I assume tlie hon. minister wishes to have.

I recognize that there is a great deal of force in what my hon. friend says, and the committee have displayed a great deal of indulgence in the matter. But it is entirely unavoidable. I have been giving a good deal of attention to this measure outside of the House, almost every spare moment I could get, in obtaining the views of railway people and of those who have special grievances, and who thought something ought to be done In this Bill to remedy them. I have listened most carefully and attentively to what they have had to say on all sides, and wherever their suggestions have commended themselves to my judgment, I have given them effect. It is the general desire, I think, on all hands lhat we should have the Bill in as workable a shape as possible ; and my intention is, immediately after it passes this committee, to have the Bill reprinted and put into the hands of hon. members ; and after it is reprinted, if hon. members will take the trouble to go over it, and desire to have any section reconsidered, or to be informed on any question connected with the Bill, I will not place any obstacle in the way. I invite suggestions from the members of the committee, and I shall be glad, when they have the whole measure before them, to have them call attention to any defects which it exhibits.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would suggest that the Bill be reprinted and distributed to the members of the House before it passes through the committee, so that they will have an opportunity of looking over it and making suggestions before it is reported to the House.

I think what the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has suggested would be desirable in addition to the reprinting of the Bill ; that is, whenever there is a material amendment to be moved, the minister should hand to the leader of the opposition one or two or half a dozen copies, and thus a good deal of time could probably be saved.

On section 213-bell and whistle on locomotive,

Before that section is passed, I desire to move an amendment. There is a certain danger to property adjoining a line of railway from which under existing conditions there is really no escape. There has been a good deal of discussion in reference to cattle-guards. Sufficient cattle-guards are necessary, but people owning stock have an opportunity of taking some reasonable precaution to protect their cat-

tie, even when there is an insufficient cattle-guard, by preventing them straying on the public highway. There has been a discussion of the subject of drainage, and there is a reasonable opportunity to the owners of land to have their property drained by an application to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. But there is a danger arising from fire occurring from sparks and cinders escaping from locomotives from which the farming community have no protection. The difficulty lies here. Most of the locomotives which are in use in this country are not equipped with proper and sufficient fire screens.
The hon. gentleman is not speaking to the clause under consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, I am proposing to amend that clause by providing that the railway companies shall equip their locomotive engines with proper fire screens.

That amendment will come in better on subclause E of clause 24, which was allowed to stand, and which deals with devices on engines to avoid fires. I would ask my hon. friend to hold his amendment over until we go back to that clause.

speechtext:
I have no objection to keep my amendment back at the hon. minister's request and on his assurance that I will be given an opportunity to present it when the clause he suggests comes up for consideration.
On section 225,
_ A watchman shall be stationed at every crossing where two main lines of railway cross each other at rail level and no train shall proceed over such crossing until signal has been made to the conductor or engineer thereof that the way is clear ; provided always that in the case of an electric street railway car crossing an electric street railway track, it shall be the duty of the conductor, before crossing, to go forward and see that the track to be crossed is clear, before giving the signal to the motor-man that the way is clear and to proceed.

I move to revise that so that it shall read :
No train or engine shall pass over any crossing where two main lines of railway cross each other at rail level until a proper signal has been received by the conductor or engineer in charge of such train or engine, from a competent person or watchman in charge of such crossing that the way is clear ; provided always that in the case of an electric street railway car crossing any railway track not otherwise properly protected, it shall be the duty of the conductor before crossing to go forward and see that the track to he crossed is clear, before giving the signal to the motorman that the way is clear and to proceed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The necessity of having a watchman at the crossing Is a matter of implication. You say the engineer shall not cross until be has received a signal

from the watchman or other competent person in charge that the way is clear. Do you think that is as good as it was before ?
It is better or I would not suggest it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is not as explicit.

I do not put the responsibility on the watchman but on the train hands and on the people who are crossing. They must not cross without this signal. The company will see to it that they have watchmen in charge because they cannot cross until that signal is given showing that the coast is clear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I know what the argument is, but I think it would be better as it was before.
Would it not be better to expressly declare what the amendment proposes by implication that a watchman shall give the signal?
There must be a signal given and the train cannot cross unless it is given.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would it not be better to say that the signal must be given by a watchman stationed at the crossing ?

In the first place he is not stationed at the crossing, and besides that there are various other means of sufficiently protecting a crossing than having a watchman. There are electric signals and bells *which are being very generally used and which do not necessitate the actual presence of a watchman. We want to have a sufficient signal no matter by whom or by what means it is given.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I am thinking about is not only the signal to the train hands, but the signal to any one approaching the crossing. There might be danger in that case, and a warning should be given to those approaching as well as to the train hands unless this section is only to apply to a railway crossing where there is no highway.
Where there are two railways crossing one another it is a particularly dangerous thing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: As a rule there is no highway at such a crossing, but there might be.

There might be but it is not customary. The railway companies try to avoid it if they can.

['Well, we can say that the hon. gentlemen were very good last evening, and I wish they would go on being good. However, if they refuse, I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.\nSome resolutions reported.']
May I ask the right hon. gentleman to give us some information respecting this.

My hon. friend will see from the map all the posts marked which we have at present in the North-west Territories, and there are some new ones on the Mackenzie river. They extend from the frontier of Manitoba along the boundary line and are chiefly in the McLeod district. There are altogether eighty different stations. We have a new post at Athabasca lake and we are building a post at the mouth of the Mackenzie river. Inspector Considine left in the month of May last to install a station there. The duties of the Mounted Police are well understood. We thought at one time that we might decrease the force but we have found it extremely difficult in view' of constant applications from the settlers. This appropriation is for 500 men at $800 a year per man, including maintenance pay and everything else. The force is composed of : one commissioner, stationed at Regina; one assistant commissioner; nine superintendents ; 24 inspectors ; 2 surgeons ; 70 sergeants; 30 corporals and 363 constables. The pay of the commissioner is $2,600; assistant commissioner, $1,600; superintendents, $1,400 each; inspectors, $1,000 each; 1 surgeon at $1,200 and one at $1,400 ; sergeants from $1 to $2 a day; corporals, 85 cents; constables, from 50 cents a day to $40 a month. In addition to the two surgeons we have to call in contract surgeons whom we pay at the rate of $60 per month and who are allowed to engage in private practice.

speechtext:
How many Indian scouts ?

North-west Mounted Police-pay of Yukon force. $170,000.
How many men have we in the Yukon ?

We have an increase of $50,000 in that item. Two or three days ago I had to take an appropriation of $150,000 to cover the expenditure of this year. These estimates were taken for 250 men, but some eighteen months ago we received notice which turned out to be true that a sort of conspiracy had been hatched at Skagway with the intention of rushing the country. They were said to be American

sympathizers, but I think really they were simply men of more or less loose morals who wanted to make a raid upon the Yukon. We sent an additional force of fifty men, but nothing came of the affair. I am sorry that we have not found it possible to withdraw these men. At present we have thirty-five posts in the Yukon between White Horse and Fort Cudahy, including two posts on the Dawson trail behind Pyramid harbour. These men do almost everything. They assist in the collection of the royalties, the collection of customs; they assist the bush rangers, the timber inspectors, the magistrates; they guard the court-house and the banks; they serve notices and do all kinds of work, and I am glad to say that the reports we have of them are very satisfactory. I do not foresee that it will be possible for us to decrease this force, and the total appropriation of $500,000 means about $1,600 for each man.
Do they receive additional pay for extra work 7

Yes. What is the pay of the force serving in the Yukon ?

I am going to give it now. One assistant commissioner, at $1,600; two superintendents, at $1,400 each; nine inspectors, at $1,000 each; four surgeons-two at $1,400, two at $1,000; special allowance to sixteen officers, at $1.25 per day each; command allowance to the assistant commissioner, at $2 per day; twenty-two sergeants, at from $1 to $1.50 per day each; special allowance, at 75 cents per day each; twenty corporals, regular allowance, at 85 cents per day each, and special allowance, at 50 cents per day each; two hundred constables, at an average of $1.10 per day each; forty-two special constables, at an average of $50 per month. In addition, there is working pay for mechanics, &c., for which we make a special estimate of $12,355.

No.
For instance, they deliver the mails and collect customs duties. Is there not an allowance made by the other departments for this work ?

1 am sorry to say that I see no possibility at this moment cf decreasing the force. 1 think myself that the force might be somewhat decreased in the older settlements in the North-west Territories, and, that in the near future we must compel these settlements to take care of themselves. But at present when we take men from the older districts, we require them farther north, and I cannot say that we contemplate any reduction in the force for some time to come.
