What is that for ?
Expenses in connection with messengers and the House generally.

I would like to draw the attention of Mr. Speaker to the fact that in one of the rooms which is used by six members, there are only two lamps and there are no desks, only plain tables. There is not a place in which we can put away any papers. I applied to the sergeant at arms and he said that he had no authority to furnish anything. Then I applied to Mr. Speaker, but whether he forgot all about it or not, we have not seen any improvement since. We ought to have some better convenience for doing our work. At least we should have sufficient lights, and it would be only right to furnish desks or some convenience for putting away papers.

I may say with regard to the desks, that they are generally supplied by the Public Works Department and are not under the control of the Speaker, though, of course, we may make some time some small expense in connection with buying desks. As a rule, however, they are under the control of the Public Works Department, and I think that I did call the attention of the department to my hon. friend's complaint and will be glad to do so again.

When we apply to the Minister of Public Works he says that he has nothing to do with it, and when we apply to Mr. Speaker, he refers us to the Public Works Department. One shifts the responsibility on to the other and we do not know where to go. It used to be the sergeant at arms who had to do with these matters, but he has nothing to do with them now.

There has been no change in that respect. Last year the room now occupied by the members from Toronto was furnished by the Public Works Department. I do not think that we ever supplied any of the rooms with furniture. All the new rooms we had last year were supplied by the Public Works Department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And the lights also ?
We can get the lights supplied by our own staff, and I shall be very glad to have justice done to the hon. gentleman and see that he has a sufficient number of lights.
We shall be very grateful. I notice that the room occupied by the Toronto members is very well furnished. I have no objection to that, but I think that others ought to be treated in the same way.

The other day I was in the room of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries and found it very badly furnished. I suppose he would be very glad also to have some changes made, and I shall be glad to do all in my power with the limited means at my disposal.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I see that the estimates of the sergeant at arms in 1897 was $33,858, and it is now $40,800, an increase of $7,000.

The explanation. I am told by the chief clerk, is that we estimated for a session of one hundred days, and now we are estimating for a session of one hundred and thirty days. But we are not spending more money; in fact we are spending less this year.

I presume this is, about the only opportunity we have of speaking our minds to the hon. Speaker of the House. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has referred to the furnishing of room 56, of which room I am one of the

occupants. Of course, we all like to have good furniture, but I am always afraid to advocate anything in the line of extravagance, or even generous expenditure, because we find it our duty to be constantly telling the government to keep within reasonable limits. Therefore, though I want to make it clear that I hare great taste for really good furniture-for elegant furniture, if you like-still, having regard to the fact that this is an extravagant government and liable to err on these lines, I wish to be distinctly understood as saying nothing whatever about it.

I desire to bring the attention of Mr. Speaker, though I do not know whether it comes within his purview to the disgraceful condition of the bathrooms downstairs. I give credit to those who deserve it for what has been accomplished in the way of improvement within recent years. At the same time, the place is nothing to what the House of Commons should have. The whole arrangement down stairs is very unsatisfactory. Another point is with regard to the messengers of the House. Messengers with impunity use the washroom set apart for members of the House, and associate with members. And I would draw the attention of the Speaker to the fact that many of these messengers impose upon two or three good-natured ones of their own class. The large amount of work is done by very few, while the others sun themselves in ease and luxury.
I am glad the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) has called attention to this matter.
I do it publicly.

I never knew the complaint made before, but I will give instructions suitable to the case.
Library of the parliament-salaries and officers of the library, $17,462.50.
There is an increase here of $332.50.

I understand that this is for the regular statutory increases.
Legislation-general-printing, printing paper and binding, $125,000.
There is an increase of $15,000 here.

That item is not entirely under my control, but is more under the control of the Joint Committee on the printing of parliament. But I am informed that this increase is due to the fact that the number of volumes that we have to print has increased. The expense in connection with the vote is simply in payment of the Printing Bureau for the printing of our documents.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is any of the printing done outside ?
No, it is all done at the Printing Bureau.
What percentage of all our printing is done in the Bureau ?
I cannot give that information. I can only speak with regard to the printing done for the House. Ail the money expended last year was expended with the Printing Bureau.

A discussion took place in the Upper Chamber the other day, and I was surprised to learn the large percentage of public printing that is not done in the Bureau-about 50 per cent if my memory serves me well.
No.

I think there was a trifle over 50 per cent done outside. It has always seemed to me that either we should have our printing done at the Printing Bureau, or we should have it done some other way. I do not think it is justifiable to allow a portion of the work to be distributed amongst the newspapers, very often at extravagant prices. There can be no doubt that, as the figures have been analysed by those who are experts in these matters, the price we pay for outside printing is very high. If the Bureau is not large enough, we should enlarge it; if it has not plant enough we should provide more plant. But we ought not to continue the dual system of having a Printing Bureau and still have work done outside.

The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is entirely wrong in the supposition that 50 per cent of the printing of parliament is done outside of the Bureau. As a matter of fact nearly all the printing of parliament is done in the Bureau. It does happen, once in a while in a congestion of work, owing to the lateness with which the reports are prepared, one or two of the departments find it necessary to get their work done outside. I agree with the hon. member for East Grey that, as far as possible, the public printing ought to be done in the Government Printing Office. But I do not agree with him in his statement that when we do go outside we pay extravagant or extortionate prices. I think that the prices obtained from outside contractors will compare very favourably with the cost of work done in the Printing Bureau.
Mr. S'PROULE. I remember that an analysis was made some time ago, and the facts as set forth by those who might be regarded as experts in printing showed that the prices of work done outside were nearly double of what we paid at the Bureau. As to the statement that only a small proportion of the printing is done outside of the Bureau, that does not agree with the figures given in the Senate the other day. I am sure that my memory is not so far astray.
It included newspaper advertising.
It is true that it included advertisements in newspapers, but it was pretty nearly 50 per cent o-fi ail we paid for printing and publishing.

That is where the hon. member (Mr. Sproule) has been led astray. He has not separated the two accounts. In the Auditor General's Report appears what is paid to each newspaper receiving the government patronage. But a very large proportion of that is for advertising and not for printing.
What is advertising but printing ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Parmelee) as chairman of the Printing Committee, says with fair correctness, that the printing of parliament is done in the Printing Bureau. But if he takes into account all the printing done for the government, he will find the statement of Sir Mackenzie Bowell-who is a printer and usually scrutinizes these matters carefully-made in the other House is in accordance with the statement of my hon. friend from East Grey, that the government printing done outside the Bureau amounts to more than that done in the Bureau. Here is the statement as published :
Sir Mackenzie Bowell stated that the extent to which the government had carried the abuses of the patronage system had run high up into the tens of thousands of dollars. One paper in Montreal had received $100,000 and could not exist without this patronage ; one of the ministers was deeply interested in it, it even being stated that he was a director.
I presume that it is the Minister of Agriculture, who is a director of the Montreal 1 Herald,' and the Montreal ' Herald ' received last year over $100,000 for printing for the government.
He gave figures, showing that in five years this paper had received $97,790, entirely in contravention of the Act. He read a few of the sums paid newspapers supporting the government. During the year ending 30th of June, printing and advertising cost $383,164, while the departmental printing cost $383,000.
When our hon. friends opposite sat on this side of the House they condemned the Conservative government because a little printing was done outside, but now we find that they have paid out $383,000 to outside newspapers. and $100,000 to the Montreal ' Herald.' of which one of the ministers is a director.
So that government papers received a little more than the legitimate printing at the bureau. The Halifax ' Chronicle,' once Mr. Fielding's paper, received $8,853 in the year ending 30th of June, 1902; the St. John 'Telegraph' received over $18,000, of which $17,000 was for lithographing, which the law provided should be done at the bureau ; the Winnipeg * Free Press,' well known as the Minister of the Interior's organ, received
$2,693. Mr. Templeman's paper only received $490, but he did not grumble, as in outlying districts all printing could not be done at the bureau.
Now, there was a charge made in the other House that this government was not only violating their pledges but violating the law as well, in order to give patronage to papers in which it is openly stated by Sir Mackenzie Bowell, in the other House, that ministers are interested, one in the Winnipeg ' Free Press,' one in the Montreal ' Herald,' and besides, there was the Finance Minister's paper, though he did not know wThether it got any of the printing.

I remember last year the Minister of the Interior distinctly claimed that he had no interest in that paper, I know nothing at all about the Montreal ' Herald.' But I rise to call attention to the fact that these papers do no printing, perhaps they may do some lithographing. But what the papers get is largely for advertising for the Department of Public Works and other departments. I know myself, so far as the 1 Morning Chronicle ' is concerned, that they do no printing, they have no printing department, they cannot print anything except the paper. It is for advertising and perhaps lithographing that these sums are paid out, and they cannot be put down in the same category as printing done at the Bureau. I do not know whether the Bureau is as well equipped as it ought to be, but I think we ought to be careful in increasing it, for the reason that a large part of the work it has to do must necessarily be done during the time parliament is in session; and to put on a large plant that would not be busy all the year round might not be the best course for the government to adopt.

The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) is not correct when he says this is all for advertising. He must surely remember that only last year the Postmaster General told us that a large portion of the work belonging to the Post Office Department was done in Montreal.
I only spoke of the Halifax ' Chronicle,' I know nothing about the other papers.

Weil, I was speaking with reference to advertising as well as printing, and the statement I made was even under the mark, for I find that we paid about $300,000 a year for work done at the Bureau and we paid $383,000 for work done outside the Bureau. Therefore, when I said that we paid about fifty per cent of the money that is paid for that kind of work outside the Bureau, I was under the mark, because instead of fifty per cent we paid a good deal over that. My complaint is that this work ought to be done in the Bureau

if we pretend to keep up a Printing Bureau for the purpose of doing government printing.

In reference to the Montreal ' Herald,' would any gentleman pretend to tell me that $97,000 was paid to that paper for advertising alone ? Now, it looks to me rather suspicious, to say the least, that a paper in which the Minister of Agriculture is a large stockholder-we are informed he is a director of it-should get so large an amount for printing. That paper is undoubtedly patronized by the government of which he is a member.
It looks very fishy.

I think it is more than fishy. It looks as if there were some suckers around that department. I should think the government would feel rather ashamed to face that fact, that a paper in Montreal in which a minister of the Crown is a large stockholder-and I challenge contradiction of the statement-but whether a stockholder or not. that paper is getting $97,000 for printing. The Chairman of the Printing Committee tells us it is for advertising. Now, I think the hon. gentleman will take that back and correct his statement. I say that the rule should apply that where so large an amount of money is expended in printing it should be let out by contract. All things being equal, I am not disposed to criticise the government for letting their friends have it, I am not disposed to criticise the government for spending small amounts to papers that are supporting them, as the papers do something for it. But when it comes to paying nearly $100,000 I say they should draw the line, and retrace thteir steps, and rectify the mistakes they have made during the last seven years.

Hon. gentlemen on the other side persist in confusing accounts that are paid for printing and accounts that are paid for advertising. As a matter of fact, a very small portion of the public printing is done outside the Bureau, and when it is done outside the Bureau it is because the Bureau is congested with work and is not able to turn it out in proper time and shape. The Bureau is fairly well equipped. As everybody knows, this is a growing time, and during the last ten or fifteen years the amount of printing' done for parliament has probably doubled, while the Bureau has not been increased in order to keep pace with the increased public printing and the printing of all sorts in connection with the departments of the government. Now, when the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) says tbat the Montreal ' Herald ' has been paid $100,000 a year for printing and advertising, he does not make the distinction between printing and advertising. But I venture to say that he is entirely wrong in his figures. The
Montreal ' Herald ' has never been paid any such amount.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: For five years.
Well, I think the hon. gentleman did not make that very clear.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I read Sir Mackenzie Bowell's statement in the Senate.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say it was for one year. For five years, possibly he is in the main correct. But I can say this, that all the public printing done outside the Bureau has been done at reasonable prices, and not at fourteen prices, as we know were charged some years ago by printers who did printing for the government when our friends the enemy Were in power.

I think that is quite a gratuitous statement. In analysing these accounts, we found that in some cases the parties were paid double prices and treble prices for printing, and to say the government get value for it, is to say what we did not find by actual inquiry when we had the accounts brought before us. As to the statement of the hon. gentleman about the very small percentage of printing done outside, could that hon. gentleman tell us how much of it is done outside ? I have heard some similar statements made in that connection in this House, but when we come to look into them closely we find that they are not borne out in fact at all but that the very reverse is the case and that a very large percentage of this work has been done outside. I remember that one or two years ago the statement was made that there was practically no printing done in connection with the department of the hon. Postmaster General and that afterwards the hon. Postmaster General himself admitted that a large proportion of the work was done in Montreal. Hon. members, when speaking upon a subject of that kind, ought to speak of What they know and they ought to give the source from which they get their information, because we want rather a reasoned judgment than the ipse dixit of any hon. member.
The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is absolutely wrong in so far as he charges that exorbitant prices were paid to the Montreal ' Herald.'
I did not mention the Montreal ' Herald ' at all. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) need not put up a man of straw and then knock him over.

Some hon. members have been alluding to the accounts of the Montreal ' Herald.' The accounts of the Montreal ' Herald ' were investigated before the Public Accounts Committee last year, or two years ago, and they are being investigated at the present time, and I venture to say that the committee will find that only fair and reasonable charges have been made
5274

in connection with that expenditure. It was proved before the House, and the statement was made by the Chairman of the Printing Committee, that the Hamilton ' Spectator ' had received fourteen prices for job work which was let out by the late government. On general principles X believe that the Bureau ought to do all the printing that it is possible to do, and I believe that is what it is doing at the present time. If the hon. gentleman will take up the report of the King's Printer, he will find that he repeats the complaint that he has made year after year that the facilities at the Bureau are not adequate for turning out all the printing that is required to be done for the various departments in connection with the printing of parliament. The Bureau, at the time it was erected, was too small to meet the demands made upon it, and with the increased demands which have arisen since then, it is absolutely impossible to turn out the work required by this parliament. I am not justifying the giving of work to outside offices unless it is absolutely necessary. In regard to the charges that are made, hon. members must remember that these are for lithographing work as well as printing. The Bureau does not do lithographing work. Lithographing work is a separate branch of printing, and has to be done in outside offices. I venture to say that if hon. members make an examination of the accounts in the Public Accounts Committee, they will find that the charges made for work done are the ordinary charges for commercial work in any city in the Dominion.

It is very refreshing to hear the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) give us his little lecture. He is an hon. gentleman, I believe, who is eminently capable of that kind of thing, but in dealing with a business matter it may, perhaps, be better to deal with it upon some business basis. For any hon. member of this House to get up for the purpose of making the plea that years ago some government paid a large price for work similar to this, is to make a very poor plea indeed. I think if the hon. gentleman cannot make a better plea on behalf of the government than to go back to the olden days aud resurrect something without proof, as a matter of fact, -but, even if you admit it to be a fact-if he cannot give any better argument than that, he only weakens the case that he endeavours to support. It is not a question at all of what other governments have done. This government came into power pledged that they would do a great deal better than any government which preceded it.
So they did.

Hear, hear.
Mr. FRASER, And they had not much of a task.
Is there anything the matter with hon. gentlemen over there ?
Keep cool.

I can keep cool. I want to say what meets with the concurrence of every sensible business man, and it is that it is time we were done absolutely and for ever with this miserable, petty plea brought forward from time to time, ' you did the same thing.'
You had better set an example on that side of the House.

I do not know to w'liat the hon. gentleman alludes. He may think he makes a telling point by that, but I cannot see what relevancy it has to what I am discussing. If the hon. gentleman contends that this is a good and proper method, why then, I feel to a. certain extent set down and knocked out, and for this reason : The hon. gentleman is a very high authority on all questions, on business questions, on questions of printing, on questions of morality, and I believe on questions of religion, but I do not understand him to seriously contend that is a proper course for any government to pursue.

In reference to printing, the hon. member for West Huron made the statement that I referred to the printing done by the Montreal ' Herald.' I never spoke of the Montreal ' Herald ' at all. What I referred to was a sheet distributed for immigration purposes and which was brought before the Public Accounts Committee. I think, if I remember correctly, that sheet cost something like $800 or $1,000 to print. I have heard from practical printers, who have been in the business for years and years, that we paid more than three prices for that work. It was, I think, literally admitted that there were very large prices paid for it, even by hon. members on' that side of the House wrho were trying to put up the best possible defence they could at the time. If we are to regard this as an example of what we may expect to find in other branches in connection with government printing, I said that we were justified in coming to the conclusion that we were paying out a very great deal of money for printing and that we got very little in return.
Contingent expenses in connection with voters' lists. $20,000.
What is that to be used for now ?

I understand that when we approach the end of parliament, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery has to provide for more expenses in connection with procuring and printing of the voters' lists. That is the reason why the amount is larger than the amount voted last year.
Why do you want any more than you had last year ? You will not print any more voters' lists.
I understand that when the parliament becomes older, when we come near the end of the parliament, as next year we will be very near the end of the parliament, we are supposed to expend more money.
I suppose that is to provide for the coming elections, because, otherwise we would not want to spend $20,000 upon the lists this year. They will not be held until two years hence.

Mr. Chairman, this is an item that we used to hear a good deal about, and we were told that it was all going to be changed when we adopted the voters' lists that are provided by each of the provinces. I used to hear a good deal about the expensive Dominion franchise, when hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side of the House. That is one of the items they used to hound us about when the party that I support was on the ministerial benches. You have a Dominion Franchise Act now under which the voters' list is provided, in the province of Ontario at least, of which I am speaking, by the municipalities. These lists are corrected by the judges and revised in readiness for an election at any time. Now, we have the same expense exactly and there is not a word from the government side of the House in reference to that expense, not even from the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) who used to challenge this expenditure and point out to the House and to the electors how extravagant it was to spend all that money when it could be remedied. He has applied the remedy, and he sits smiling to think that the same amount of money is being expended that he denounced when in opposition.
It was awful in those days.
You are spending twice as much and. it is all right.
This amount is too little to print the voters' list and too much to print the lists for the by-elections.
I understand that it was the unanimous wish of the House some years ago that the lists required for byelections should be printed.
Are some of your members to get lucrative jobs ?
Not that I know of.
Judging by this large vote the only explanation is that a lot of these hon. gentlemen opposite are going to get their reward.	,

There cannot possibly be a dollar required for printing the voters' lists in Ontario or any of the older provinces where the lists are made up each year. It might be that in Manitoba you would require to print the list for a byelection, but certainly not in the other provinces.

I understand that the Bill as introduced did not provide for the printing of these lists, and at the request of the Hon. Mr. Montague an amendment was made providing that this printing should be done.
Is this printing done outside of the Bureau ?
No. All the printing for the House of Commons is done at the Bureau.
I understand that you have to pay a certain sum to the clerks of municipalities for furnishing these lists ?
The clerk of the Crown in Chancery buys these lists every year. This is provided for by law.

The preparation of the voters' list for the Lisgar election cost $5,080.4(1. If that is to be the price for each constituency then the system under the late Conservative government was much less expensive. The commissioner who had charge of the work in Lisgar got $600; thirty-five registration clerks, $1,137; tjhe Winnipeg ' Free Press ' for printing $875.64. Some one appears to have applied the pruning knife because the accounts rendered amounted to $7,321.2S and the amount paid was $5,680.40. It is a most monstrously extravagant way of proceeding. In this case you are asking a vote of $20,000 and that would provide for three or four by-elections even in the province of Manitoba. If the elections are held in other provinces I cannot see where the expense comes in.

I have no information with regard to the Lisgar election, but I will be happy to get it for the hon. gentleman.
Mr. OSLER, Is there any reason why there should be an increase this year from $12,000 to $20,000? Was the vote sufficient last year ?
It was sufficient last year, but I am told that at the end of a parliament it is customary to take a larger vote for this purpose.

There must be something ill view or surely you would not increase this vote more than double. It seems to be out of all reason, but seeing the pleasant smile of Mr. Speaker, I suppose we will have to let this pass.

I cannot understand why Mr. Speaker says that this vote

is increased at the end of a parliament. The rule is that there are more by-elections at the beginning of a parliament than at the end of a parliament.
In the past it has been customary at the end of each parliament to take a larger sum for this vote and we are simply following the precedent.

1 admit that the last session of a parliament would provide a larger amount for by-elections than the session immediately after a general election. If this vote is taken in expectation of a general election, it is all right.
I understand that a certain amount is provided for the first year, and a certain amount for each subsequent year, as required. It is gradual.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
We are ready for a general election.
To pay customs and other officers for services in compiling and forwarding daily reports in connection with the Fisheries Intelligence Bureau for the season 1902, $270.
What is that for ?
This amount is voted every year. These reports give us information in regard to the United States fishing fleet. The allowance of each officer is placed at $15.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
In item 10 of the main estimates I find :	' Salaries, including R.
E Tyrwhitt at $950, and L. Bance at $1,400, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.' I would like to inquire of the minister when this Mr. Bance went into the department, if he has passed the qualifying examination, and why he is receiving $1,400 salary.
That item has been voted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood that we could ask any question we liked on these estimates, and I want to make this inquiry. I want to know who this Mr. Bance is, and why he is put over the heads of older officials.

Mr. Bance was recommended by the officers of the department as an expert French translator. He has been in the department eleven years, and has had charge of all the French correspondence of the department, and he was recommended for a first-class clerkship. The amount was recommended by the minister and voted by the House when the item was called.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Did he pass the qualifying examination ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AID
FISHERIES. I am informed that he passed
all the examinations.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I am informed that he did not pass the qualifying examination.
^ The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. I am informed he did. I will inquire and give the hon. gentleman the information.
Fisheries-further amount required for construction of new steamers in British Columbia, $9,000.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND I' ISHERIES. In 1901-2, $50,000 was placed m the estimates for the construction of a steamer in British Columbia. Of this amount $11,290 lapsed. The vessel has been completed and has been accepted by the department-the ' Kestrel '-and the amount due is $9,000.

What was the total cost of the ' Kestrel 1
' The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. Seventy-two thousand dollars.
Was it built by contract ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Are there any steamers engaged in the fisheries service on the lakes ?

I gave a list at a previous sitting of the committee. There are two vessels employed on the lakes, the ' Petrel ' and the Bayfield.' The 'Bayfield' is on the Georgian Bay or Lake Superior, and the ' Petrel ' is doing fisheries service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understood that the 1 Bayfield ' was sold.
We sold the old 'Bayfield.' The new 'Bayfield' used to be the 'Lord Stanley.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I regret that I did not hear the statement of the hon. minister the other night in regard to the fishery inspectors in the province of Ontario. Will he kindly tell us what the duties of those inspectors are, and why they are maintained, since the Dominion government has surrendered its right to control the fisheries, and what their functions are.
We went over this question at the last sitting of the committee, and I thought we had covered all the ground.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What are the duties of these officers ?

They were stated so many times in the last sittings of the committee that I did not think that it would be necessary to repeat them. According to the

judgment of the Privy Council, the fishery rights and privileges belong to the provinces but the Dominion government must see to the enforcement of the laws and regulations; and pending a settlement of the difficulty between the Dominion and provincial governments, we are carrying out the judgment of the Privy Council as interpreted by the Department of Justice. Three inspectors or overseers have been named for Ontario. Their duties are to see that the regulations are carried out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Last year we were told that we were on the eve of a settlement.

The government is prepared for a settlement. All that is required is an agreement between the provincial and the Dominion governments for a submission of the case to the Supi'eme Court, so as to have a legal interpretation of this judgment.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Would it not be better to reach an agreement by a conference ?

That is rather difficult. The best mode is to agree on a case and submit it to the1 Supreme Court for interpretation. We had representatives here from the provincial government on the question of increased subsidies, and during the conference this question of the fisheries was discussed, and we decided that a submission of a case to the Supreme Court would be the most reasonable way of arriving at a settlement.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Do these officers visif the various localities and fishing centres ?

If the hon. gentleman will read their report in the blue-book of the Marine and Fisheries Department of 1902. he will make himself familiar with what they are doing. They are obliged to go around the districts assigned to them and see that the regulations are observed in the lakes and rivers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I happen to come from a riding where there are a great many inland lakes, and I have never heard of any of these gentlemen visiting them. These lakes extend for a chain of 150 miles, and you might as well look for a needle in a hay stack as try to detect any infraction of tlie law by sending an inspector there. The only way would be to have local officers appointed, who would live on the lake shore and could see from their window what is going on. If the hon. minister wants to know what these gentleman do, I can tell him that some of them take a very active part in elections. I have seen them at work in my own riding, and perhaps their labours in tha-t respect have been charged up.
There are many local inspectors appointed by the provincial government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Did the hon. minister find out anything about that $100 to which I referred the other evening ?
There was nothing paid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

If he did the work, he must hnve been paid. The hon. gentleman surely does not expect me to carry in my head payments made two years ago. I have my officers and they have to look into the books to find out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

You gave me notice about a man named Collins and now it appears the name is Mullen.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND BTSHERIES.

' I find in the Auditor General's Report for 1901-2 an item C. Mullens, Belleville, for the season of 1901, $33.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where ?
In some of the waters of that section.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
That is a portion of the payment. The hon. member for West Hastings says that the arrangement was that C. Mullens should get $100. He was promised a job and he got it.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND

the job.

Mr. Hurley had nothing to do with it.

He got it by open tender.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

Yes.

speechtext: The hon. minister will remember that I brought the matter up the other night and the statement was made that Mr. Hurley was the means of having a protest entered against the hon. member for West Hastings. And I understood from the statement made in the House that the protest was made by a man named C. Mullens. After that statement had been made in the House, the hon. minister in charge of the department notified Mr. Hurley, and Immediately got an affidavit from Mr. Hurley, the fishery inspector, who was charged with having arranged for this protest, declaring that there was no truth whatever in the statement that he had promised Mullens $100, or any other amount. It was taken for granted that that affidavit was true. But now we find that Mullens was engaged in accordance with the statement made by the hon. member to put out these buoys, and he was paid for doing the work, and this is shown by the Auditor General's Report. Of course, it does not show in this one item an amount of $100. Now, the worst part of the whole matter is that the payment of this man proves that the statement made by the hon. member for West Hastings was true and that the affidavit of Mr. Hurley was false, and I would like to have the minister state if these are not the facts in their proper sequence.

No sfieh inference can fairly 166
be drawn from the facts as that drawn by the hon. member (Mr. Reid, Grenville). A man gets a contract in fair competition to do some work for the department. At first it was said to be one Collins ; now it appears that it is Mullens. Mullens and Collins are so mixed up that there is neither head nor tail to the statements-
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister need not work himself up in this fashion. Mullens was the man.

Then let it be Mullens. If the information possessed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid, Grenville) about Mullens is as accurate as that about Collins, some hon. members of the committee will draw their own inference. It seeihs that Mullens' name has been mentioned in connection with some transaction that I know nothing about, and that nobody seems to know anything about. The mere fact that a man gets $33 for services to the department, service that is rendered in the ordinary way, does not show anything whatever. Mr. Hurley Whose name has been mentioned, has had nothing to do with it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: How does the hon. minister know that ?
It is not part of the duties of Mr. Hurley to have anything to do with these matters. There is an officer of the department in charge -of the buoys. Mr. Fraser, I think is in charge of this service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that this was done by tender and contract. Will he bring down the documents ?
I have already told the committee that I will bring them down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. minister makes light of this because I mentioned the name the other evening as Collins. But the hon. minister who had charge of the department'followed it up by speaking of the man as Collins. It is treating the matter in rather a small spirit to try to wiggle out of it by dwelling on the mistake of names. Now, Mullens is prepared to make affidavit that the agreement was what has been stated, notwithstanding what the minister has said, and notwithstanding the affidavit of Mr. Hurley, produced here last session.

Since questions have been asked in regard to the steamers employed on the lakes, I would like to ask the hon. minister with regard to the steamer ' Bayfield,' employed on the Georgian bay. I have a few questions on the Order Paper, but I would like the hon. minister to answer them now, if convenient ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND
FISHERIES. I have the answers to the

questions ready, and X have sent for the paper. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thomson, Grey) desires, I will be able to give him the information in a moment.
I understand that a steamer has been purchased lately for service on the St. Lawrence, a steamer named the ' Alaska.' What is she to be employed at ?
I will get the information more definitely. I know there was a small boat bought lately to do the work of sweeping out the channel between Montreal and Kingston.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understood that the steamer ' Scout ' was on the river.
The ' Scout ' does not do this work of sweeping out the channel, but a different class of work entirely.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
How many fishery overseers are appointed by this government for the province of Ontario ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Three inspectors and overseers, they are the same thing.

Where do they live ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Hon. gentleman will find full information regarding these officers by reading their reports, which are to be found on pages 12 and 13 of the report of the department.

Where do they live ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	ANDFISHERIES. Mr.	Hurley lives at	Belleville, Mr. Duncan at Marchville, Out., and Mr. Shepherd at Toronto.

Is this inspector Hurley that has been referred to so frequently, also an official of the Ontario government ?
The MINISTER OF1 MARINE AND FISHERIES. I do not know that he is.

I understand that these three men, employed by the Dominion government, are also deriving an income from the Ontario government. I am not prepared to prove that, perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would be able to tell us definitely whether that is the case or not. But we have the fact that Mr. Hurley is receiving from the Dominion government $1,200 a year, and we have also the fact that he received $255.51 for travelling allowances, making a total of $1,455.51 for the period of one year. I find by looking at the Public Accounts that during that year Mr. Hurley also received for expenses in connection with the census of the Dominion of Canada. $155, and for revising the

returns, w'hatever that may mean, $178, making a total for that item of $333. Now, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is new in the department that he has the honour to preside over, and we expect that he has come to that office with a great deal of ardour to do what is night and to remedy any evils that he may find. I hope I have only to call his attention to the fact that this official has been receiving two salaries where he is only entitled to one, to see the hon. gentleman set about at once to remedy the evil. I am sure he will come to the conclusion that it is a most iniquitous thing to allow that gentleman, while receiving full pay and travelling allowances for services as fishery inspector to receive in addition this $333. I assume this money has peen paid, and perhaps the minister would not be able to control it. But I point out to the minister a remedy that is In his own hands. We are voting the full allowance for his salary, and out of that salary it would be proper for the minister to deduct this $333. In this way the minister will have an opportunity to show him that no official v in his department, at all events, shall be paid twice over for his services.

I understand a steamer has been purchased, as the minister States, to be employed in sweeping the channel. Now the minister will find on inquiring in his department that the steamer ' Scout ' was built by the government two or three years ago, and at that time it was stated that she was to be used for the placing of buoys between Montreal and Kingston, and to look after the channel generally. Now this steamer the ' Scout,' is well adapted for that purpose, because she was built for it. But the minister knows that if she only looked after placing the buoys she would not have more than two weeks work in the whole season. She is running up and down the river between Montreal and Kingston, and could easily do any sweeping of the channel. She is better built than any other boat for that purpose. I have not the slightest doubt that this new boat, the ' Alaska,' which is being put on by the government will create an extra and constant expense. I would like to have some further explanation given whether he really means that the ' Alaska ' is merely to be used to follow the ' Scout ' up and down the river, and is being used practically as a pleasure yacht during the whole season.

I was misinformed when I told the committee that this boat had been bought. She has been rented for six or seven weeks for the purpose of sweeping the channel, a work which the ' Scout ' cannot do. Now we have retained the services of the captain of the ' Alaska,' and have put on some men of the crew of the ' Scout ' to help the ' Alaska ' -in the work she is

doing in sweeping the channel, which is of a temporary character.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Then I understand that the statements publicly made around the St. Lawrence that the ' Alaska ' has been purchased or is to be purchased by the department, are not correct ?

They are absolutely incorrect. The amount expended on repairs to the ' Bayfield ' during the last six years was $0,571.89. The steamer ' Bayfield ' has been sold to Messrs. John Harrison & Son for $3,250, the highest offer. The intended disposal of the ' Bayfield ' was generally known and that was the only favourable offer received. The sale was confirmed by Order in Council on the 14th of March, 1903.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
We have expended $6,571 for repairing this vessel within the last six years and we sell her by private sale for $3,250. I do not think this is satisfactory. I am sure that when the matter goes out to the people of North Grey it will not create a favourable impression in the minds of the friends of the hon. gentleman	opposite in	that	vicinity.	What
makes it more deplorable is the fact that this boat has been sold by private sale.

Was the sale made since the hon. minister came into the department ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. It was made on the 14tli March, 1903, after I came Into office.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
By tender ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. As regards	the repairs that
were made to the boat, if we had been obliged to charter another boat there it would have cost more than $6,571. The boat was found in such bad condition that it was considered better to dispose of her than to continue spending money in repairing her.

What was the justification for selling that boat by private sale Y
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. It was well known since last fall that the boat was for sale and we had many offers. The highest offer which was received near the opening of navigation was that of Messrs. John Harrison & Son and after consultation with the officers of the department who recommended that the sale should be made, the offer of Messrs. Harrison & Son was accepted.
What is the length of the ' Baj-field ' ?
92 feet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I happen to have known something about this vessel for years, and I 166}
must say that I am surprised that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, right at his entrance to office, should have performed the act he has, namely, of handing over this' boat to a party friend and a strong partisan without public competition. This boat, I am bound to say, if it had been offered for sale on the open market, instead of bringing $3,250 would have brought twice that amount. . She was a vessel with heavy machinery and a vessel which for many years had been kept in first class repair. This boat has been employed on the surveys on lake Superior and Huron and the Georgian bay, putting out in all kinds of wind and weather and yet the hon. minister as one of his first official acts does this : Without exposing this boat to public competition and sale, without giving any notice to the general public that the boat was for sale, allows pressure to be brought to bear upon him by party friends and practically makes a present of this boat to party friends, Messrs. Harrison & Sons, who are the strongest party friends the hon. gentleman has in the town of Owen Sound. This is oniy on a par, except that.it is more exaggerated, with the job that was perpetrated in the same town a few years ago when the steamer ' Petrel ' was handed over to a party friend and I think it was Mr. Harrison who got it. I think I am right in the name, but perhaps it was a different man. The hon. minister must give some information to the committee as to what steps he took in the public interest, not in the interest of Messrs. Harrison & Sons and some party friends up there, to find out what was a fair price for this boat. Who made the report as to the value of the boat ?

The report as to the value of the boat and the condition in which she was, was made by Mr. W. J. Stewart the officer in charge of the hydrographic survey. He condemned the boat, and he refused to go to Lake Superior in her. That boat has never done service on Lake Superior as she was unfit for such service. He informed the department before I took charge that another boat should be procured. The ' Lord Stanley ' would have gone on the survey on the lakes during the season of 1902. if she had not been rented to the Department of Public Works for the trip made west by the late Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte). It was well known all over the country that the ' Bayfield ' was unfit for service and that she was unfit for sale. Mr. Stewart tried to sell her and asked for offers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Where was the boat employed last year ?

At the entrance to Lake Superior, but she could not go into the lake and that is the reason why Mr. Stewart

recommended that she should he replaced by another boat and that she should he disposed of. We found the [DOT] Lord Stanley ' ready to undertake that work. She had been undergoing repairs in the works at Sorel. It wras recommended by the officers of the department that we should ask for prices for the * Bayfield we looked around, we got different prices and we sold her to the highest bidder.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Who else put in tenders for the boat besides Messrs. Harrison & Son, since the hon. minister has said in the most emphatic way that after looking around and receiving a number of tenders they found that of Messrs. Harrison & Son the highest 7

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) must not put words into my mouth that I did not say. I said that there were offers made. I know of one in particular, although 1 do not remember the name, that was made to me. I consulted Mr. Stewart in regard to it, and Mr. Stewart said to me: You had better wait as we may have a better offer than that. After that we got this offer of Messrs. Harrison & Sons and after a good deal of discussion about it during which we tried, as I remember perfectly well, to get a little more, we accepted the offer. I consulted the hon. ex-Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) who knew more about it than I did. He knew the circumstances of the purchase of the ' Lord Stanley ' to replace this boat. After due consideration the ' Bayfield ' was sold to Messrs. Harrison & Son for the price which has been mentioned and the sale was confirmed by Order in Council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Well, there is nothing very astonishing in the minister making a statement that the sale was confirmed by Order in Council. Surely, if the hon. gentleman's colleagues had any confidence in him, when he made his report, they would confirm it. 1 am not reflecting on the hon. minister directly or suggesting that he profited by the sale, but I do say, that the hon. minister gave an exhibition of weakness when he permitted his party friends at Owen Sound to crack the whip over his head and force him into doing what was wrong. The hon. minister knows very well that he is not disposing of his private property but the property of the people of the Dominion, and that he has no business to give this property to his party friends because pressure is brought to bear upon him to induce him to make the sale. I can tell the hon. minister that if there had been a public sale this boat would have brought twice the amount he received for it and it lies at the door of the hon. minister that lie has been a party to a wrong act on the part of his department towards the people of this Dominion in allowing himself at the Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
crack of the whip in the hands of party friends in the town of Owen Sound to dispose of a property that was worth double the amount for which it is sold. As an excuse the minister tells us that Mr. Stewart reported that the vessel was unfit for service on Lake Superior. I can well believe that Mr. Stewart would not care to trust the lives of himself and his men in that boat on Lake Superior during the late fall. But the fact that a boat is not fit for service on a tempestuous lake is no reason why she should be handed over to a party friend at his own price. There are other lakes where she could be utilized. On the shores of the Georgian bay where this boat is well and favourably known it will be an excellent piece of campaign literature when we are able to tell the people that the government practically made a present of this valuable steamer to a party hack.
I am glad the hon. gentleman has something to find fault with the government for.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I corroborate what has been said by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) I was asked to place this question on the Order Paper because in the town of Owen Sound no one knew to whom the boat was sold or what she was sold for, and that will give an idea of the publicity which the minister gave to the sale of the ' Bayfield.' She is a magnificent steamer in first-class repair, and if she were put on the market she would bring double the price the government received for her. I do not know of any better campaign literature for the Conservatives than to be able to showr to the people the reckless and improvident manner in which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the government transact the business of the country.
Mr. HUGHES Victoria). There is a more important side to it than a [DOT] mere piece of campaign literature. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries must remember that he is merely the servant of the people and he will have to learn that he will not get off with impunity when he perpetrates jobs like this. What qualification had Mr. Stewart to pronounce on the fitness of this boat.
He is a surveyor.
He is not an engineer at all. Who is this Mr. Stewart 7
He is a good Conservative; he is not a supporter of this government.

Mr. Stewart is the engineer in charge of the hydrographic survey of that part of Ontario. He is an old employee of the department and if the hon. gentleman will look at ' Hansard ' he will find that some years ago Mr. Stewart was praised

by Sir Charles Tupper himself as being one of the ablest engineers in the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: For valuing ships ?

Oh, well, I do not think it takes any extraordinary ability to value a ship of that kind, since we have got the opinion of the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) who put a value on it, and also the member for North Grey (Mr. Thomson) who said it was worth double what we got for it. I am informed by my officers that Messrs. Harrison & Son were so dissatisfied with the purchase that they wanted to return the boat and get their money back a few days after the sale.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Oh !

Any ordinary business man would have sold this boat by public tender, and that is what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should have done. I want a direct answer to the question why he did not advertise this boat for sale; also the amount of money expended on her for repairs twelve months prior to the sale.
I have answered that for the last Six years $6,571.89 have been spent on her for repairs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: How much last year ?

It is an average of about $1,000 a year. I have not got the books of the department here and I cannot say what was spent on her last year, but I can get that information. If I had been asked for the expenditure for one year I would have obtained it and given it just as readily as for six years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister did not tell me why he did not advertise that vessel for sale.
Purely and simply to avoid expense.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Oh !

Hon. gentlemen do not seem to recognize what it would cost to advertise an article for sale in a dozen or two dozen or perhaps three dozen newspapers. The boat was pronounced worthless by the officer and if we spent $1,000 or may be $2,000 in advertising-
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Rot.

It might cost $2,000. If we advertised only in the Liberal papers we would be censured and if we advertised in all the
newspapers it would cost a very large sum. I am informed that the engineer is a most respectable and a most efficient officer. He reported to me that the vessel was worthless and seeing that it would cost so much for advertising, offers were taken, and I remember that one was lower than the offer of Harrison & Son.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Who is that ?
I do not remember the name.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I must confess that the defence made by the minister for the disposal of this boat in such a way is a mighty weak one.

Let me ask the minister some things that he can tell. He tells us that it would cost a matter of $2,000 or $3,000 to advertise this boat for sale in the newspapers. That in itself indicates the extravagance of this government. Although the hon. gentleman is new in the department I presume he knows something of the inward workings of the government, and when he tells us that it would cost this large amount of money to advertise the sale of a boat he knows that the government is accustomed to make such reckless expenditure. It is something for the people to pause over and think about, that a Minister of the Crown, when dealing with a piece of property that he wants us to believe was only worth $3,000 pledges his position as a Minister of the Crown that he honestly believed it would cost from $2,000 to $3,000 to advertise in the newspapers the sale of that vessel.
He did not say that. He said from $1,000 to $2,000.

It does not make the slightest difference whether it was $1,000 or $2,000. Put it at $500, if you like. It illustrates the same extravagant way of dealing with these questions, the same want of either judgment or candour. It must be well known to any business man that in a port like Owei) Sound, and in the neighbouring ports of Midland and Collingwood, having in them men who would be open to a reasonable transaction such as the purchase of a vessel like this, it would be amply sufficient to advertise in one newspaper in each of these towns at an expenditure of $10 or $15, perhaps not more than $5, in order to ensure an ample number of tenders-not from servants and supporters of the government, but from honest men willing to give a fair price for a good vessel such as this was. I say it does not commend itself to the common sense of this committee, and it will not commend itself to the common sense of the people when it goes forth, that a minister of the Crown in order to bolster up a bad case, tried to lead us to believe that the advertising of this vessel would cost $2,000.
Will the minister tell us how he would advertise that vessel to make it cost $2,000 ?
Go to the Montreal ' Herald.' That would cost $1,000.

I do not think the Montreal ' Herald ' would be the proper paper in which to advertise the sale of a vessel in the Georgian bay. I think if it were advertised in the ' Globe ' and the ' Mail ' and in a trade journal, that would be sufficient, and that would not cost more than $25 or $50. When the minister, in order to defend this deal, which is a deplorable one, gets up and states that it would cost $1,000 to advertise the sale of that vessel, his case is very weak indeed, and I am sure the country will view it in that light.
What did the minister do with the furnishings '! Did they go with the ship V
They were put on the other-vessel, the new ' Bayfield.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. minister stated a few minutes ago that the reason he did not advertise this boat was that he wished to save expense. Now, this government profess to be a business government. I ask the minister how any farmer would dispose of some surplus stock which he wanted to-get rid of. He would go to a printer and get out one hundred or two hundred handbills. If the minister had done that, it would have cost $2 or $3, or perhaps $5. He could have sent these to his officers at Midland or Owen Sound, and they would have distributed them. These hand-bills would have announced that this boat would be sold by public auction on a certain day, and there would have been competition in purchasing her. The people of this country trusted the minister with that piece of their property, expecting that when it was no longer fit for service he would get the most he could for it. Did he do what any practical business man would have done, who had some surplus stock which he wanted to get rid of ? Hon. gentlemen who know that boat say that it is worth two or three times what the hon. minister sold it for to one of his political friends. I will guarantee that the engines and boilers of that boat could be sold for as much as the hon. gentleman got for the whole vessel. The bare fact is there, and the country can see it, that the hon. gentleman has handed over a valuable piece of the people's property to a political friend for half its value. He said he had another offer, but he does not remember who made it. Is it not on record in the department ? This whole transaction is an outrage, and the opposition will not he doing its duty if it does not bring in a motion censuring the government for it. Instead of putting the boat up for sale by public auction or tender, the hon. gentleman receives in a corner of his office this gentleman from Owen Sound, who wanted this boat for a particular purpose. and lets him have it. I venture to say that there was not a business man in Owen Sound who knew that the boat was for sale, except this political friend who wanted her for a special purpose, and the government handed the boat over to him. This is the way this business government, who nrofess to be an honest government, are trafficking politically with the property of the people of this country. I would feel untrue to my position. as a representative of the people, if I were to see the public property sacrificed in this way without making a protest. Is there a minister of the Crown who will get up and justify the course followed, or say be deals in this way with the people's property ?
/
The hon. minister said he had a lower offer from another party. What is the name of the party -who made that offer ?
I do not remember the name but will furnish it to the committee tomorrow with the report of the engineer aud everything else.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has the hou. minister the offer of this man and the report of Mr. Stewart ?
Of course, all papers connected with the sale will be put before the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has he not also a letter from Mr. Harrison wanting him to take the property back and shedding a few tears over it ?
No, it was Stratton who shed the tears.

This would not be so objectionable were it not the second time that the same thing has been done in Owen Sound. Only the year before last there was another transaction of a similar nature. The 'Petrel' was sold for about $2,000, and I have a letter in my possession saying that it was sold for one-third its value or less. Had an advertisement been put in the paper at Owen Sound, which would have cost fifty cents, that boat would have brought $5,000 or $0,000. I brought that transaction to the attention of the House, and I asked that in future, whenever any property belonging to the government was to be sold, some public notice should be given so that the country might get a reasonable return. This year we have a similar transaction again. The ' Petrel ' was bought by one Harrison, not the same gentleman who has bought this boat, but also a strong friend of the government. I ask again that in future some public notice should be advertised. I have a letter in my possession with reference to this boat, which says distinctly that if it bad been known in Owen Sound that she was for sale, she could have been sold for three times the money, but that nobody was made aware of the sale. We have sold this boat for $3,250 and have paid $50,000 for another boat to take her place. This boat had been kept up from year to year, and a few years ago it was stated that she was practically as good as new. She was in splendid repair and in good condition, and this is the first time we ever heard of her being otherwise.

In the Auditor General's Report for last year, I find that over $3,000 was spent by the department on this boat in one year. On this same steamer, the ' Bayfield,' $3,000 were spent, according to the report of the Auditor General, in 1901. In the report of 1902, I find the following
expenditures on the steamer ' Bayfield.' John Harrison got $66 out of her; Carey & Co., London, got $107.80; Lewis Rice & Son, Toronto, got $102; A. M. McGregor, was paid $140 for labour of fitting her out; Maitland Rixon & Co., got $18.50 for lumber; Andrew Malcolm, Kincardine, got $35 for oak wainseotting; John Nisbit, Owen Sound, got $605 for labour, and the North American Bent Chair Company were paid $1,850 for work and supplies of all kinds for this boat; and Rickard Bros., of Owen Sound, for painting and graining, received $203. Yet in the face of the fact that all this money was spent last year, over $3,000 on this boat, the hon. minister was so weak that when his friends came down and cracked the whip over his head, he sold her to them for $3,200. I would ask the hon. minister this question, whether a deed of a certain water frontage in the town of Midland has been granted to Pratt & Co., coal dealers ?
It is under consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I can tell the hon. gentleman how much under consideration it is, that the parties have already erected a $20,000 dock on the property-a property which the town had bought on the understanding that the piece in dispute would pass to it. What is the consideration these people are paying ?
I have stated that this water front has not been granted, and the hon. gentleman has no right to ask me what consideration has been paid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I asked what consideration is in the deed. The parties have made an offer to the department which the department is considering. What is the money consideration which has been offered for this water front ? What money consideration has been offered for this water frontage ?

These things are done in different ways. Sometimes a person applying for a foreshore makes an application purely and simply for a foreshore, leaving it to the government to decide the amount to be charged for the concession. Others make a direct offer, which is taken into consideration by the government. In this case, I think there was no direct offer made by these gentlemen. That is probably the reason why the matter is under consideration, because we must learn what value we should put upon the concession.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I can state, for the benefit of the hon. minister that

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think that we shall arrive at anything definite by departing so widely from the question before the Chair. The item under discussion

is tlie amount required for the construction of new steamers in British Columbia. I cannot see the connection between that and the foreshore in Midland.

We shall hear more of the foreshore. The hou. minister shall hear more of it in that town. And the hon. minister must have given a promise, because these people have erected their dock at the cost of $20,000 on this property. Going back to the question of the vessel. I think a good deal is to be said as to why the minister should be voted money to construct vessels. He has some good vessels-that is, his department has, though he seems to regard them as his own-and he accepted a great deal of responsibility when he permitted his party friends to force him (I am charitable enough to believe that he must have been forced), to sell this vessel for $3,200, when no less than $3,000 had been spent in repairs upon her only last year. Had there been a fair, honest, open, aboveboard sale of this vessel, she would have brought, as my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) said, three times that amount. I am sure that the vessel, from what I have known of her in the past, and knowing that $3,000 was spent on her last year, would have sold for far more than double the amount that was actually obtained for her. So long as the hon. minister is in the position he now occupies, if he conducts the affairs of his department in this unbusiness like manner, he deserves, and, so far as I am concerned, he will receive, the censure of this side of the House.

I am sorry I was not here when this discussion commenced, and so have not had the advantage of hearing all that has been said. But 1 would recall to the attention of the minister some statements he made on assuming the office that he now holds. We had the statement from him that it was the intention of the department to establish the nucleus ofj a Canadian navy and to have training ships on the great lakes, and also on the Atlantic and the Pacific. It seems to me that, if it is the intention of the government to establish a naval force on our inland waters, the government lost a golden opportunity when it failed to retain this vessel to be used as one of its training ships. She was a staunch vessel, sea-worthy in every particular, and in view of the fact that $3,000 of the people's money had been spent, only a few months before, in putting her in good repair, it was little short of criminal not to retain that vessel as one of the means of making the nucleus of a navy upon the lakes. I reiterate and reaffirm what has been said by my bon. friends on this side, that this transaction was most unbusiness like .and most unfair to the country, that a vessel that has done such service as the ' Bayfield ' has done, and that has been maintained in a state of efficiency year after

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: year at the expense of the country, when being put out of commission was not offered publicly for sale, so that the people interested might have an opportunity to bid upon her. If this practice is to prevail, and 1 am afraid, from what I can gather, that it prevails in other departments of the public service-the public money must be frittered away instead of being spent to the best advantage. Business methods are not being adopted by this so-called business government in directing the affairs of the country. I am sorry that the minister has neglected a manifest duty In not endeavouring to get the highest possible price for this vessel if her term of public service was to be closed. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman what he is doing towards establishing a naval service on the lakes ? Does he intend to have training ships ? If so, will he buy second-hand vessels, or does he intend to get some out-of-date vessels of the imperial navy in order to establish this naval force on our inland waters as well as upon the ocean ?

The matter of the naval reserve is under consideration. It is being studied, just as the question of the militia reserve is being studied. I do not think that anything practical will be done in reference to this matter before next year. The two projects require a good deal of study as to the cast involved and as to how the whole scheme is to be carried out. So, we have not considered yet whether we shall buy old vessels or construct new ones. That is a question upon which information must be gathered, that wre may establish the military service upon the best and most advantageous conditions
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I must call the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) to order. I do not think the discussion upon which he has entered has any relation to this item. Therefore, I would ask the committee to come back to the item and discuss the propriety of voting the sum of $9,000 for constructing new steamers in British Columbia.

I must come to the defence of the hon. minister. I have a very distinct recollection that when we were dealing with these items in the main estimates, a general discussion was not gone into at the time, because it was said that when we came to the supplementary estimates, In dealing with any one item, we could travel over the whole field, and discuss not only this branch of the service, but the other. Therefore, I respectfully submit that any member of this House is justly entitled to travel outside the record of this particular item.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
And we are discussing
item 93, which covers not only this amount,
but several others, and opens up practically the whole service of the department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course, if there has been an agreement between the minister and the committee as to liberty to be granted in this discussion, I do not wish to interfere. My business is to point out the rule, and allow the minister to make his own arrangement.

To return to the point under discussion, I do not require the amount expended on the vessel last year, for the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has given that from the Auditor General's Report-over $3,000 spent in repairs of this vessel last year. Yet, she is sold by private sale for no greater sum than was spent in repairs for one year. It is possible for a minister to make a mistake, and for one mistake we would not criticise very severly. But this kind of thing has been repeated. The hon. minister will not even tell us now that such a thing will not take place again. When the estimates for supply were under discussion the other evening, we found out that he was paying from one hundred to one hundred and fifty per cent more for supplies than would be charged in any retail hardware store. We asked him if he would publicly call for tenders in future, and he would give us no satisfaction, but said in effect, that he would do as he liked in the matter. X think it is to be regretted that an hon. gentleman holding so high a position in the government of Canada should allow the funds of this country to be frittered away in the manner which characterizes the administration of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Will the hon. minister bring down the names of the gentlemen who tendered for this vessel ?
I said I would.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: No, he said he would bring down the letter of Mr. Harrison.
I beg pardon, I said I would bring down all the papers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What preliminary conversations or .correspondence did the hon. gentleman have with this Harrison Arm about this ship ?
I did not know them, never saw them in my life.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I think the minister has -carried on the deal at somebody else's direction. Who gave him the direction to make this deal ? We would not for a moment charge the minister with knowing anything about Owen Sound people. It must be some one in Ontario that
arranged the deal. I would like to know all the particulars that the minister can furnish us.
There is another pertinent question. I would like to know if the Liberal candidate in the late byelection was the one who recommended the sale of this vessel at this figure ?
I could not tell the hon. gentleman. I never saw the man in my life, and had no communication with him, directly or indirectly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am simply asking the question : Was the sale of this vessel recommended by the Liberal candidate in the late by-election ?

I repeat that I have had no communication [DOT]whatever with the gentleman to whom the hon. gentleman alludes. I do not know him at all, received no letters from him, had no correspondence with him whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Who recommended the sale of the vessel ?
Mr. Stewart recommended It.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Was it the minister who recommended the sale of this vessel to Harrison and Sons ?

I took the responsibility, along with my colleagues, on the recommendation of the officers of the department, who told me the vessel was useless, and that the sooner we disposed of it the better; that the price offered was fair and reasonable, and that it was the highest price that we could get for it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Were the officials who, in 1891, advised the expenditure of $3,000 on this vessel to put it in first class repair, the same officials who tell him today that this vessel was useless ?
