It was repaired in the previous season to do the work in the next season of 1902, and the officials stated that it would cost more than $3,000 to charter another vessel. The fact that $3,000 was spent on her during the season of 1901 shows that the vessel must have been a very poor one to require such extensive repairs in order to fit her for the season of 1902. She would not have been put in commission, I am informed, in 1902 if the ' Lord Stanley ' had not been used by the Department of Public Works.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will the minister answer why he recommended that the vessel should be sold by private sale instead of by public tender ?
Because I thought it was in the public interest to do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Did this whole transaction occur by accident ? Did the minister receive, without any previous communication, a letter from Mr. Stewart saying : You had better sell this vessel to these gentlemen, it is the best we can do; it is true we have not asked anybody to make a bid, but if we can get $3,000 it is my advice to take it and get rid of her as quickly as possible ? I would like the hon. gentleman to answer that question. Does he think that was a business-like proposition that this vessel, on which more than $3,000 had been expended the previous year, was no good after that, or that she was only worth $3,000 ? The hon. gentleman has said that $3,000 was spent on the vessel the previous year. What was it expended for ? The hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) read out some of the items of the expenditure, including wainscotting put in the cabin. Were thirty-five men required to do duty on her as a crew in the previous season? Are there any reports in the department as to the condition in which the vessel was at the end of navigation in 1902 ? Surely if the hon. gqntleman hopes to pose as the equal in business capacity with his colleagues in the ministry, he will have to make a better showing than he does in this business. How does it happen that this transaction was done behind doors ?

If the hon. gentleman had been here at the beginning of the discussion he would have heard what I have repeated several times, that when I entered the department in the fall of 1902 they were considering the service for the next season, and it was recommended to me by the officials of the department that we would have to replace the steamer ' Bayfield ' on the survey on Lake Superior, by the ' Lord Stanley,' which had been bought the year previous especially to do that service. Then in providing for repairs of the different steamers belonging to the department, nothing was provided for the steamer ' Bayfield ' because it was recommended by the officials to dispose of her. That is what I learned in the department. Mr. Stewart, I understand. the engineer in charge of the hydrographic survey in that part of Ontario, tried, as he informed me. to sell the boat. He notified, I think, everybody that he met that the boat was for sale. That is the report he made to me.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: A report in writing ?

Yes. I have said that 1 would bring all these reports before the House. Everything was done above-board. Hon. gentlemen will see by the papers that the whole transaction was done in good faith Mr. THOMSON fNorth Grey).
and as I have sand just now, for the sake of the .public interest and nothing else. If the officers had supposed that they would be able to sell the vessel for a higher price by advertising her for sale, they would have advised me to that effect. But that would have entailed considerable expense, and we would not get a cent more for the vessel. Under these circumstances, when we received the offer from Harrison and Son, we took the precaution to get more reports concerning the vessel, and it was after their offer had been in the department for a few days that the matter was closed. I consulted with the officer who Had been in charge of this part of Ontario, who is one of the most competent and honest officers in the department. After taking all these precautions, if anybody thinks the department has been cheated, well, I could understand there would be a reason for prolonging this discussion. But 1 do not see that there was anything out of the usual course except that public tenders were not asked for, and they were not asked for because they would have entailed a large expenditure. We sold the vessel under the best conditions possible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Are the government steamers inspected by government officials every year, their boilers, hulls and so on ?
I forgot to mention that the vessel was condemned by the inspector.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Will the minister bring that report down to-morrow ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. Yes.

What is the name of the vessel that was put on in place of this one ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. The 'Bayfield.' It used to be the ' Lord Stanley.'

What price was paid for the ' Bayfield ' ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. I am informed the ' Bayfield ' was bought in 1902 for $45,000.

I understood the minister to say a moment ago that the very fact that $3,000 was spent on the former steamer in repairs -in one year was proof that she was no good. I cannot understand that reasoning at all. I understand there is $1,000 being spent now on tfiis new boat, so that, according to the hon. minister, she is very rapidly deteriorating. I would like the hon. minister to explain this line of reasoning in saying that $3,000 being spent on a boat proves that she was no good.

My reasoning is very simple and

any one would understand it except the hon. gentleman. It depends entirely on the value of the boat. If you put $3,000 on a boat that is not worth more than $3,000 it is a waste of money, but if you put $10,000 on a boat which is worth $50,000 and improve her by so much it is not a waste of money if you make her suitable for the service she is required to perform. The ' Lord Stanley ' was repaired at the works at Sorel in order to tit her for the work she was intended to perform on the great lakes. There had to be special rooms provided for the engineers, a special surveying bridge, and the necessary apparatus to do the work that she was destined to do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: How much was spent on this vessel at Sorel ?
I think between $8,000 and $10,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not understand the reasoning of the hon. minister. It seems to me that if the argument which he has advanced in regard to expending $3,000 on the ' Bayfield ' holds good, we have a serious charge against him for purchasing this vessel called the ' Lord Stanley.' He tells us that the boat cost $45,000 and that they expended $8,000 in repairing this vessel at Sorel. I find in the Auditor General's Report that the Poison Company received $3,200 for further repairs to the ' Lord Stanley,' which makes over $11,000 expended on the ' Lord Stanley.' This vessel cannot have been in very good repair. Now, we are not complaining about the purchase of the ' Lord Stanley,' but when the hon. minister declares that he sold the ' Bayfield ' in the public interest we claim that he did not, because, if he had sold it in the public interest he would have sold it by tender and not by private sale. A dollar would have paid for an advertisement in the Owen Sound newspapers, it would have brought a number of people interested in the sale together and the result would have been that the vessel would probably have brought three times the amount he received. I do not consider that the hon. minister was acting in the public interest in disposing of that vessel by private sale. I would ask the hon. minister why he purchased the 'Lord Stanley' if what he says about the ' Bayfield ' is right and why it was neeessary to spend $11,000 in repairing that vessel before he could put her into commission.

The same officers who recommended that we should offer for sale the steamer that was perfectly useless, recommended that thp ' Lord Stanley ' should be repaired. As regards the repairs made at the Poison Company, it is very easy for an hon. gentleman to pick out an item and make a great fuss about it. These repairs were purely and simply the result of an accident
by which the boat broke her propeller. She had to be repaired and we paid the market price for these repairs. She also injured her stern post.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister say that it would cost $3,200 to buy a new propeller ?
And a stern post.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understand the hon. minister is prepared to bring down some data to-morrow, I should like to have the report of the inspector of hulls, boilers and engines.

I will bring down all the papers I have. If I knew what papers were in the records of the department I would say at once what they are. I know there are reports in the department on this question and I will bring them down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: There should be reports in the department for every year during which this steamer has been in commission. The reports of the inspector of hulls and boilers and the history of the vessel should be in the hon. gentleman's department in black and white, and I want them.
You shall have them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And I want more than that. I understand that there is the old ' Bayfield ' that has been sold and there is a new ' Bayfield II.' Was ' Bayfield II ' formerly the * Lord Stanley ' ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I want the history of the ' Lord Stanley ' also.
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I want the reports of the engineers which are in the department, showing the condition of this vessel each year for four or five years back.
I cannot give it for four or five years because we only bought the ' Lord Stanley ' last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: No matter when the hon. minister bought her. The hon. minister did not buy her on the American side. If she has been in commission in Canada, her record is in the department.
We have the record of the boat in the department, but as regards any history of the boat I cannot undertake to give the history of a boat that was not the property of the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Every one horse tug boat in the country has a history in the department.
What history does the hon. gentleman want ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The nature of the ship, her dimensions, tonnage, and the condition of her hull and boilers.
That is published in the public documents.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I would like to have brought down here the history of these two vessels for five years back.
The history of these vessels is all in the reports of the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: We want it.
It was put before the House at the beginning of the session.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. minister said that to expend $3,000 on a vessel like the ' Bayfield ' was practically a waste of public money. Am I repeating correctly what the hon. minister said ?
Considering her value.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I understand from the hon. minister that the officers who recommended the expenditure of that $3,000 which, according to the hon. minister was a waste of public money, were the same officers who recommended her sale after the money had been expended on her for $3,000.

I told the committee, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) had been here, that the officers of the department in the year 1901 recommended that this boat should be put in commission in the following year and that she needed to be repaired. They considered that in wasting $3,000, if I may so term it, in repairing the boat they were doing right because they had no other boat at their disposal. If they had chartered another boat it would have cost them $6,000 or $8,000 according to size and suitability of the steamer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Were these the same gentlemen who recommended the purchase of the * Lord Stanley ' !
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman if they were the same persons. We have in the department many officers and they are not all consulted at the same time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Is it not rather a serious situation that a vessel like the ' Lord Stanley,' purchased for $40,000 or $45,000, should Hon. Mr. PREFONT AINE.
immediately require an expenditure of $12,000 or $15,000 upon her to fit her for the services that she was to be engaged in ? We want information as to her tonnage, her engine power, the condition of the boilers and so on. If the minister admits that we wasted money on the ' Bayfield ' last year then we have the right to scrutinize most closely the expenditure which the minister is about to make on other vessels.

The ' Lord Stanley ' was built in England or Scotland as a very strong tow boat. We bought her from Davie at Point Levis for $45,000, and I think she cost over $80,000. She was in perfect order as regards engines and hull, and everything connected with her, but we had to fit her out for the special work of the hydrographic service adding an upper deck and chart house.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is she larger than the [DOT] Bayfield ?'
I am informed that she is about double the size.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is the ' Lord Stanley ' 220 feet ?
I am informed she is twice the strength and about twice the size of the ' Bayfield.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Oh, no.
Was there any particular reason why the name should be changed V
No, except that we wanted to retain the name of ' Bayfield,' who first started the hydrographic survey in Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will the minister be good enough to give us the report recommending the repairs- to the ' Bayfield.' He told us that information was laid on the Table at the beginning of the session. In what was the information contained.

The report of the department was laid on the Table of the House which contains reports of steamboat inspectors. The inspection of Dominion steamers of the department is made by an officer specially appointed for that purpose. It is not deemed necessary to publish his reports but they are on record in the department.
Mi-. HUGHES (Victoria). It shows nothing of the kind. The minister must understand that his smirking anchsmiling will not get his estimates through. The people of this country may submit to being robbed and skinned and fleeced for a time, but the opposition will let the minister know

about it. I must say in all kindness to tile minister that I do not like the manner in which he tries to smile the matter off. The people of this country are supposed to run this little show and if the minister does not understand it we will teach him. He is there only temporarily.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Permanently.

No. We will be over there in a little while and then the business of the country will be run properly. I want the report recommending the $3,000 expenditure on this ship within the last year. Will the minister bring that down.
I said so ten times.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Is the minister going to lay down the policy that he will dispose of a vessel belonging to the government for the amount she cost in the previous year to repair. If that is his policy be should sell the ' Lord Stanley ' for $11,-
000.
Hear, hear.
Is that to be the policy of the minister ?
I have no policy in the matter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What policy did the minister adopt when he sold the ' Bayfield ' for $3,000, just what she cost to repair the previous year ?
Public interest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And sold it by private sale.
Public interest, as I have stated.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Under what item is the minister going to give to-morrow all this information that we have asked to-night. It is not that we suspect him of being slippery in trying to evade his promises, but I would like to know under what item he will give the explanation.
I never said I would give an explanation. I said I would file the documents as soon as they were copied. They will be put on the Table of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The minister will have to give the information from his place in the House and his estimates will not go through until he does.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister told us a moment ago that he would find Mr. Hurley's report on page 41 of the annual report of the department and the other night he told us that Mr. Hurley only made verbal reports. At page 41 there is the deputy minister's report in which he relates some information that I presume Mr. Hurley furnished him, but there is no report from Mr. Hurley. Mr. Hurley lives in Belleville and he knows the Americans caught bass and he told the deputy minister so, and the deputy reported it, but that is not a report from Mr. Hurley. We want to see Mr. Hurley's written reports to the department. I want the minister to explain why he made that statement to the House, that in his report we would find the report made by Mr. Hurley.
I made no such statement. I said that Mr. Hurley's report was contained in tlie report of the deputy minister.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I find in the report the deputy minister says :

Hurley, of Belleville, reports that sporting fish were very plentiful this year, especially so in the Bay of Quinte, Trent and other large rivers.
What are sporting fish ?
Surely the hon. gentleman is not going to expect me to give him a description of every fish. I will not do it, because I do not know it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
He says further :
Bass, trout and maskinonge were extremely abundant in the bay and lakes and on the rivers inland, where the coarse heads, viz., pike, pickerel, bull-fish, suckers, &c., do not go. On Trent and Moira rivers, pike, pickerel, &c., are numerous at the mouth and a few miles up the rivers until stopped by the dams. There are neither bass nor maskinonge there, hut up the rivers the sporting fish are plentiful.
I think the minister should explain what all this means, because it is nonsense to me. The report goes on :
I think the fishways would be disastrous to sporting fish in these rivers, as they would allow rough fish

Another term, I do not know what it means

-to go up, and they would infest the spawning grounds of the game fish.
What are game fish ? Then he says :
There is not enough supervision in the district. as oue overseer has over two hundred miles to look after. There should be a steam yacht for that section to enable the local officers to do their work.
Has the minister provided a steam yacht for the gentlemen to cruise around Lake Ontario V
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I hope the minister will endeavour to find out what game fish, sporting fish, rough fish, and coarse fish are ?
May I ask the minister the date of the report of the engineer condemning the ' Bayfield'V
If I knew the date, 1 would give the report.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Was there a report made last fall t>y any person condemning the ' Bayfield ' ?
There must have been. I will bring all the papers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I find in the minister's report, dated December, 1902, on page 18, the following reference to the 'Bayfield':
The * Bayfield ' is a wooden steamer 110 feet long. 18 feet wide, and 9 feet deep. The steamer was engaged in the hydrographic survey on Lake Superior during the season of 1902. Mr. W. J. Stewart is in charge of this work. Captain A. M. McGregor is the sailing master of the ' Bayfield,' and the crew consists of nineteen men in addition.
There is not a single word in this report about the vessel being unseaworthy, but it states that she had been all summer, with a crew of over twenty men, on the exposed waters of Lake Superior. The minister had better admit the corn, that the clamps were put on him pretty hard, and that he was made to give this boat to John Harrison & Son, of Owen Sound, for $3,000.

The hon. gentleman does not mean to convey to the committee that there is anything in the report stating that the vessel was seaworthy. The report only gives the list of the different boats in the possession of the department without stating in what condition they were.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But if the boat had been in such a bad condition, why did the minister not state it in his report ?
It is not the place to mention it at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That was probably the minister's view of what a report should be -to mention nothing.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The minister stated a moment ago that he had not Mr. Hurley's report. If he turns to page 5127 of ' Hansard,' he will find that he stated the other night :
I have here Mr. Hurley's report on page xli of the Blue-book.
There is nothing of the kind there.

The hon. gentleman is playing on words, just as lie plays on figures from the Auditor General's Report. What I stated was correct, that the report of Mr. Hurley is contained in the report of the deputy minister of Marine and Fisheries.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Further amount required for the Canadian Fishery Exhibit, $1,800.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will the minister explain this V
This sum is required to make necessary repairs to the fishery exhibit in Ottawa. For many years there had been no repairs, and the specimens were being destroyed and some new ones were necessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This money is to be spent between now and the 30th of June. It must have been expended already, and the minister ought to have the details.
We are fixing up everything. I would invite the hon. gentleman to visit the exhibit.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman ought to be able to tell us how he spent the money.
I have stated how it was spent. It was spent in securing specimens, installing them, overhauling and papering the room, electric light and all that was necessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must have a detailed statement.
I have no detailed statement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Surely the hon. gentleman is not asking for $1,800 without being able to furnish the particulars.
If the hon. gentleman desires such a statement, I shall produce it, but I will have to give a statement of a lot of small sums spent on repairs and overhauling generally.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It is not usual for heads of departments to ask for money without having the details.
I have not got them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then let the item stand.
I am informed by the officers of the department that the installing of the electric light, the painting and the rearranging of the fittings in the laboratory take up nearly the whole of the sum.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It is surely not a business like proposition to ask the committee to vote $1,800 on such an explanation as the hon. minister has given. He says that the installation of the electric lights and the fitting up of the laboratory have cost nearly the total sum asked for. It is not unreasonable that we should require more information.

I ain informed by my officers that there is such a statement and it will be produced at once. We will let the item stand in the mean time.
Item allowed to stand.
To pay collectors of customs for services in connection with the issuing of fishing licenses to the United States vessels in 1902, $505.72.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The officers are allowed 5 per cent, and the collection amounted to $10,114.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: We have not had a statement yet as to how this business is conducted. I understand that the Dominion regulates the size of the meshes and appoints a number of inspectors to see that the law is enforced and that no fish are caught out of the proper season. Who gets the revenue, and if it is divided, what proportion goes to the Dominion and what to the provinces ? I understood a year or two ago that it was to be paid into a common fund, and that was to be afterwards divided in some way.

The revenue for 1901-2 was as follows : Ontario, $373 ; Quebec, $3,498 ; Nova Scotia, $6,062 ; New Brunswick, $11,658 ; Prince Edward Island, $1,829 ; Manitoba, $2,279 ; North-west Territories, $946 ; British Columbia, $41,178 ; Yukon, $1,110. License to United States fishing vessels, $11,000. Total, $79,169.58.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
From what source do you receive that revenue ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. From licenses and fines.

We get no revenue from licenses in Ontario at all ?
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. No.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
You get only $300 revenue in Ontario and you are paying nearly $4,000 for salaries to the overseers.
The	MINISTER	OF	MARINE	AND
FISHERIES. We are obliged, under the law to pay it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You are not obliged to keep Mr. Hurley and Mr. Shepherd.
Mr. Hurley is a very dis-agreable person to the hon. gentleman, but he is doing good work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If he is doing such good work, would the hon. minister bring down a report of his good work 7
I think the hon. gentleman is unreasonable. It may take five or six weeks to prepare such a report.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Has he got the report in his department ?
Yes, and as soon as possible I will have it copied.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman can bring down the original paper ? I venture to say that Mr. Hurley has not spent five weeks in visiting the lakes, and it could not have taken him very long to make a report.

I was not complaining of the smallness of the revenue, nor that the work was not properly done, but was urging that at as early a date as possible we should reach some understanding with the provinces as to our rights and duties in connection' with the fisheries, and whether we are not entitled to more revenue than we are receiving. The government ought to direct its attention towards a settlement as early as possible, so that we may know what our duties are and what revenue we are likely to derive in the future.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) is perfectly right, but he should not blame the present government or the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The question was pending before the courts for nearly three years before it was finally decided by the Privy Council In 1897 ,or 1898-I do not know exactly the date. But the judgment has left the Dominion government and the governments of the provinces in much the same position as before as regards certain questions. There are certain points still in dispute, because there is a difference of opinion with regard to the interpretation of the judgment. So, as I explained, we are face to face with another case before the courts. We are trying to arrange amicably to submit a case to the Supreme Court, but that has not been decided yet. There has been conference after conference, and, as I said, there are piles of documents on the subject in my department and in the Department of Justice. Many opinions have been asked and given, but we have not yet been able to come to an understanding with the provinces. I hope that within a few days after the end of the session, we shall be in a position to submit to the Supreme Court a case upon the points in dispute. Until that Is settled, we are obliged to have a modus vivendi, and this we are carrying out in good faith* The department is most anxious that the question should be settled as soon ns possible- it is in the interest of all parties. For instance, British Columbia is making a claim upon the Dominion for a large amount. There is, no doubt, a sum of money due to that province, but to ascertain the amount, you must know what the judgment means in certain points. Meantime we are acting

as administrators for the province of British Columbia, with their consent. The question cannot be allowed to remain in the present position, for it is not fair either to the Dominion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The hon. minister seems not to be able to draw a distinction between complaining and asking for information. I respectfully submit that I have not made a complaint to-night, but I have endeavoured in a most courteous way to elicit information. And I was the more justified in asking for information to-night because practically the same statement was made last year as the hon. minister has just given to the committee, that, in a few days it was hoped by conference to have all these matters arranged. If my memory is not at fault, the decision of the Privy Council was given in 1898 or 1899. Now, is it too much to expect that between 1S99 and 1903 some understanding should be reached with the provinces with regard to this important question ? Particularly in view of the fact that we have a Supreme Court that was established for the settlement of these very questions between the provinces and the Dominion ? The government have a right at any time to state a case and submit it to the Supreme Court and ask an opinion with regard to it. This can be done at any time. Therefore, I think that there has been unnecessary delay in this matter. But in saying that, I do not want the hon. minister to say that I am unnecessarily criticising what has been done, but only endeavouring to find in what state the negotiations are for the time and when we may hope to have them finally completed.
Would the hon. minister state the points still at issue between the provinces and the Dominion on this fishery question ?

Different provinces have sent memoranda of their cases, and the Department of Justice would have to choose between the different points and claims made so as to find a common ground of discussion before the Supreme Court. I cannot give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett), on the spur of the moment, the information he desires.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is it not true that the government of the Privy Council gave the inland fisheries exclusively to the provinces? I understand that the provinces are now claiming territorial rights-that is, the maritime provinces are claiming all within the three-mile limit around the coast. That is the point, I think to be decided. Has the government of Prince Edward Island made a claim for refund of moneys collected by the Dominion ?
I know that there is such a
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: question pending between the Dominion government and the provincial government of Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: One item is allowed to stand for information that the minister has promised to bring down to-morrow. I think that, having voted so much money this evening, and having worked last night till two o'clock, we might now adjourn.

The hon. gentlemen were courteous and obliging last evening and I appreciate that. I would suggest that there are just one or two items left in the estimates of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, which might be taken up, and, if any information is desired with regard to them, the hon. minister will be ready to bring it down. I think we would make so much more progress if we proceed in that way. It is not late yet. '
I do not think the hon. minister will make greater progress in that way.

There is an item in the supplementary estimates of $1,800. I am willing to leave that there. But there is another item in the main estimates, at page Gl, item 715-construction of lighthouses and aids to navigation $322,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: But that is only one of a number of items making up item 175, and the whole are discussable upon this particular vote.
There is no objection to that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The same is true with reference to this item No. 93 of the supple-mentaries, of which this vote of $1,800 stands.

If I remember well, when this item of $322,000 was left in the main estimates, the other items had been all adopted. and this item was left because the committee wanted the detailed information with regard to the works that were intended to be carried out during next season. I procured a statement of these different works in detail. I think the item is not one that can be very much discussed-simply whether these aids to navigation are necessary or unnecessary. They have all been undertaken on the advice of the chief engineer of the department, and most of them have been asked for by the people interested in navigation. I think there can be very little room for discussion under this item.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. .

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. minister does not seem to understand my statement. Though all except this one vote were passed, it was understood that all voted in item 175 were discussable when the item came up. I know there are several members who want

to speak upon tills item 175, and some of them are not here to-night. I ask that this item stand, and also the one concerning which my hon. friend from Victoria is promised information to-morrow. We will allow the $1,800 in the supplementaries to pass, with the understanding that it will be discussable later on.
The Minister of Inland Revenue has a few items which he would like to get passed. They are not controversial, and his officers have been here for the whole evening. Take item 229.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is too heavy an item to take up to-night. There is a large increase to discuss.
I can explain it to the satisfaction of the committee. I have been waiting here all the evening to get some of my items through.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If we take it up we shall get into trouble, I fear.
I do not want any trouble, but I want fair play. I would like to pass some of these items. In fact I have been so much delayed that some of my employees will have to wait a few day's to be paid.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: We will give you money enough to-morrow.

Well, we can say that the hon. gentlemen were very good last evening, and I wish they would go on being good. However, if they refuse, I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?

The Minister of Railways will invite the attention of the committee again to the Bill respecting railways. It is a very long Bill, and we hope to make sufficient progress to-morrow almost to complete it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would suggest that the government send that Bill to a special committee. We have lost ten or twelve days discussing it now, and if the balance of the Bill were left to a committee of three or four members on each side, they' could put it into shape while the rest of the House was doing other work. We have lost, I think, ten days on that Bill, and have made very little progress, it is but little more than half way through. Let the hon. gentlemen 167
who take an interest on that Bill thresh it out in committee.
Perhaps my hon. friend will be good enough to renew that suggestion when the Minister of Railways is in his place to-morrow.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.55 p.m.
Wednesday, June 24, 1903.
